Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.title: Blazor Server Architecture and Security Guide
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.one_line_summary: A comprehensive guide covering architecture patterns (base classes, EF configurations, ServiceResult, Adapter, bulk operations), security fundamentals (roles, BCrypt, sessions, CSRF, claims), and Blazor-specific gotchas (ProtectedLocalStorage, localization, JS interop).
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.executive_summary: This 13-chapter guide walks through the full stack of patterns you need for an enterprise Blazor Server application, from DRY inheritance hierarchies and EF Core configuration classes to the ServiceResult pattern for error handling and the Adapter pattern for model-agnostic modules. Part II covers security without ASP.NET Identity using custom claims, BCrypt, session tokens, and antiforgery. Part III tackles the prerendering trap: why ProtectedLocalStorage and JS interop crash in OnInitializedAsync and must defer to OnAfterRenderAsync.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.suggested_metaphor: This guide is like a Swiss Army knife in a Blazor belt pouch: base classes are the shared handle, ServiceResult is the tiny 'did it cut cleanly?' indicator, the Adapter is the universal-bit screwdriver, and the prerendering warnings are the loud 'do NOT open during takeoff' sticker on the whole thing.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.suggested_intro_hook: You can build a Blazor app that 'works' in about an afternoon. Building one that survives its third feature request, its first security audit, and its first prerender crash at 2am — that takes the twelve decisions in this guide.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.what_it_teaches: How to structure a Blazor Server application with proper separation of concerns: inheritance for shared entity properties, dedicated configuration classes for EF Core, ServiceResult as the universal return shape for service layer calls, the Adapter pattern for decoupling reusable modules from specific user models, and bulk operations for scale. Then the full security story without ASP.NET Identity: role-permission modeling, BCrypt with salting and work factors, session tokens hashed in DB, CSRF via antiforgery tokens, and the big reveal that [Authorize] just checks Claims — you can build a ClaimsPrincipal from any user model. Finally the Blazor-specific timing gotchas around prerendering.
key_takeaways: Two-level base class hierarchy (BaseEntity, BaseAuditableEntity) removes audit-field duplication and lets you add features like soft-delete in one place
IEntityTypeConfiguration per entity beats Data Annotations and OnModelCreating mega-methods; ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly wires them up automatically
ServiceResult<T> with Ok/Fail factory methods turns service errors into first-class return values, killing both the null-returning and throw-everywhere anti-patterns
The Adapter pattern lets a module like an LMS depend on ILmsLearner instead of your concrete User class, making it reusable and extractable
BulkExtensions with SetOutputIdentity=true is 60x faster than per-row SaveChanges and returns the new IDs into your original list
ASP.NET Identity is optional: [Authorize] and <AuthorizeView> only inspect Claims, so a custom AuthenticationStateProvider that builds ClaimsPrincipal from your own User table works identically
BCrypt's intentional slowness (work factor 12 ~300ms per hash) turns a 10-hour MD5 crack into a 70-million-year BCrypt crack
ProtectedLocalStorage and JSRuntime throw InvalidOperationException during prerender; move those calls to OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender) and call StateHasChanged() after
Education/Basics/Blazor_Architecture_and.quality_notes: Very thorough — 13 chapters with consistent structure (problem, bad approaches, solution, code, benefits). Strong cross-referencing between patterns. Code examples are realistic and match the author's own project conventions. ASCII diagrams survived PDF extraction poorly but content is clear.

Education/tutorial.html.title: Build a Reactive Login Page From Zero — SVG, CSS State Machine, JS
Education/tutorial.html.one_line_summary: A zero-knowledge-required walkthrough of building an animated login page with SVG characters whose expressions and arm positions are driven entirely by a single CSS class toggled from JavaScript.
Education/tutorial.html.executive_summary: This nine-chapter course teaches SVG coordinate systems, path commands, grouping, CSS descendant selectors, specificity, the state-machine pattern (one class on one root element drives all visibility and transforms), cubic-bezier spring curves, and vector math for clamping pupils inside eyeballs. The core lesson is architectural: JavaScript's only job is to change #app.className — CSS does the actual reacting. The author explains every attribute, every operator, every math step before using it.
Education/tutorial.html.suggested_metaphor: The whole animated login is built like a traffic light controlled by a single switch. JavaScript just flips the switch (class name). CSS is the electrical wiring that decides which bulb glows. The SVG characters are the bulbs. If you ever feel tempted to reach past the switch and wiggle a bulb directly from JS, you've missed the point — and you'll spend the next two hours debugging why the green light won't turn off.
Education/tutorial.html.suggested_intro_hook: Most login pages are a noun. This one is a verb: the characters look where your cursor goes, smile when your email is valid, cover their eyes when you type your password. Want to know the trick? It's one CSS class. That's it. Everything else is just selector specificity doing the work for you.
Education/tutorial.html.what_it_teaches: How to build a self-contained interactive UI with zero framework, using SVG as a coordinate-based canvas, CSS descendant selectors as a declarative visibility engine, and minimal JavaScript as a state dispatcher. Every concept is decoded line by line: viewBox math, why <circle> uses cx/cy instead of x/y, how the Q (quadratic Bezier) command's control point direction determines smile-vs-frown, why SVG transforms need transform-box: fill-box, and how a tiny Math.min(dist, range)/dist expression handles both the 'inside the leash' and 'at the leash limit' cases in one line.
key_takeaways: SVG viewBox is an abstract coordinate grid independent of rendered pixel size, which is why SVG stays sharp at any scale
The Q (quadratic Bezier) control point acts like gravity on a curve — moving it above or below the endpoints flips a smile into a frown with no other changes
A CSS descendant selector like #app.s-email-ok .face-smile reads as 'find #app that also has class s-email-ok, then find .face-smile inside it' and reacts automatically when JS swaps the class
CSS specificity (ID=100, class=10, element=1) makes the state rule (#app.state .face) automatically beat the default (.face { display:none }) without !important
SVG transforms default to origin (0,0) of the whole canvas; transform-box: fill-box makes them pivot from the element's own bounding box like HTML elements do
cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) with Y values > 1 creates a spring overshoot — the arm flies slightly past its target then snaps back
The JS-only-changes-class pattern means if you find yourself writing element.style.display = ..., you're missing a CSS state
Math.min(dist, range) / dist is a one-line vector clamp: returns 1.0 when inside the leash, fractional when outside
Education/tutorial.html.quality_notes: Exceptionally well-written tutorial. Every single attribute and operator is explained before being used, with analogies (graph paper, leash, traffic light, folder). Has live playgrounds and demo widgets (lost in text extraction but referenced). One of the best 'from zero' tutorials in the library.

Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.title: Blazor Server For Dummies — Simple Explanations for Complex Concepts
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.one_line_summary: A beginner-friendly companion to the Architecture and Security Guide, teaching the same 13 patterns but with heavy use of real-world analogies (pizza shops, safety deposit boxes, European power adapters, festival wristbands).
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.executive_summary: This is the 'For Dummies' rewrite of the full Blazor Architecture and Security Guide — same 13 chapters across Building Blocks, Security, and Blazor Magic, but with every concept introduced through a concrete analogy and with the 'why' explained before the 'how'. Base classes become a pizza shop's 'base pizza', bulk operations become loading a moving truck, hashing becomes shredding a document, sessions become festival wristbands, and CSRF becomes a sneaky website that pretends to be your bank. Clearly part of a beginner-first learning track.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.suggested_metaphor: If the full Architecture Guide is the IKEA instruction booklet, this is the cartoon version where the little stick figure points at each bolt and says 'this one goes in the round hole, trust me.' Same furniture, gentler journey.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.suggested_intro_hook: Ever read a technical doc and felt like you needed a technical doc to understand the technical doc? This one fixes that by starting every chapter with something you already know — a pizza, a power adapter, a wristband — and explaining the C# version from there.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.what_it_teaches: The same pattern library as the full Architecture Guide (inheritance hierarchies, EF configs, ServiceResult, adapters, bulk ops, roles, BCrypt, sessions, CSRF, claims, ProtectedLocalStorage, localization, JS interop) but with a beginner-first pedagogy: analogy first, problem demo second, solution third, key point fourth, cheat sheet at the end. Also ends with a Blazor lifecycle cheat sheet mapping OnInitializedAsync / OnAfterRenderAsync / OnParametersSetAsync to 'browser ready?' yes/no.
key_takeaways: Base classes are like a 'base pizza' — define shared Id and CreatedAt once, all entities inherit
ServiceResult is like tracking for a package: every service call returns 'shipped / delivered / wrong address' instead of null or a thrown exception
The adapter pattern is the US-to-EU power converter: your LMS only knows about ILearner, so any user type plus an adapter works
Bulk operations are a moving truck — load everything once and make one database trip instead of 1000 round trips
Sessions are festival wristbands — show your ticket once at login, then flash the wristband (token) for every subsequent request
Claims are a driver's license — [Authorize] just checks if you have the right claims, and you can build ClaimsPrincipal from your own User without ASP.NET Identity
OnAfterRenderAsync is the ONLY safe place for browser-dependent calls like ProtectedLocalStorage and JS interop
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.quality_notes: Effective companion doc — same scope as the big guide at roughly half the word count. Analogies are consistently good. Code snippets are minimal but realistic. If a reader only has 15 minutes, this beats the full guide. Looks like the same content pass run through a 'friendly voice' filter.
Education/Basics/Blazor_Guide_For_Dummie.series_name: Blazor For Dummies track (paired with Architecture & Security Guide)

Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.title: Sistema de Serviço de Stock — Documentação Técnica Formal (PT)
Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.one_line_summary: Portuguese technical documentation for the BioBraga real-time stock inventory service: a decorator-cached, multi-layer tracking system using raw SQL Server functions, graduated cache expiration, preloaded Task patterns, and IDbContextFactory connection pooling.
Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.executive_summary: This is the formal technical documentation for a production stock-tracking service built on EF Core with raw-SQL access to fn_ArtigoStockByDate and fn_ArtigoUsedInFluxo. The architecture uses the Decorator pattern to wrap StockService with CachedStockService (IMemoryCache), implements graduated cache expiration (1 hour for historical data older than 7 days, 5 minutes for recent data), uses the 'task preloading' pattern in ArtigoDetalhe.razor to start expensive operations before the user clicks the stock tab, and achieves ~99.95% improvement on cached queries (2000ms to 1ms). Includes health checks, structured logging, performance metrics, and a cache-stats debug endpoint.
key_concepts: raw SQL function calls via DbConnection

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The BioBraga application needs to show article stock levels on a high-traffic detail page (ArtigoDetalhe.razor), including historical point-in-time queries. Hitting the database for every tab click and every date filter would crush the SQL Server — the document records a naive 2000ms response time on uncached queries. The business also needs accurate, temporal stock (what was the balance on 2024-01-15?) which requires a custom SQL function walking document movements with entradas/saidas aggregation. The cache layer exists to make the user perceive instant response while preserving that accuracy.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Exposes IStockService with four methods: GetArticleStockByDateAsync (temporal balance), GetStockMovementsAsync (filtered history with joins across CrmDocumentoDetalhes/CrmDocumentos/CrmTipoDocumentos/CrmSerieDocumentos), GetStockTotalsAsync (aggregated entradas/saidas), and CheckFluxoAsync (per-document-line flux). Wraps it in CachedStockService (decorator) registered via a Program.cs factory that composes both layers. On the UI, ArtigoDetalhe.razor kicks off a Task<ArtigoStock> at OnInitializedAsync without awaiting it, then awaits it when the user finally clicks the Stock tab — often returning instantly because it's already complete.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Inside StockService.GetArticleStockByDateAsync, a new DbContext is created via the factory, a raw DbConnection is opened, and SqlParameters are used to call dbo.fn_ArtigoStockByDate(@ArtigoId, @Date). The date is incremented by one day to make 'end of day' inclusive. CachedStockService first checks IMemoryCache with key stock_{artigoId}_{yyyyMMdd}; on miss it calls the inner service, then caches with expiration = 1h if date is older than 7 days (immutable history) or 5m otherwise. Complex movement queries use LINQ joins across four CRM tables with AsNoTracking and date filtering via .Where(...AddDays(1).AddSeconds(-1)) for end-of-day semantics. The UI layer holds _stockSummaryTask and _stockMovementsTask fields to implement the reuse-or-refetch pattern when filters change. Health checks verify both DB connectivity and cache hit rates (hits/misses ratio). IMemoryCache is configured with SizeLimit=1000 and 25% compaction to prevent runaway memory use.

Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.suggested_metaphor: The Stock Service is a barista with a chalkboard. Every time someone asks 'how much is a latte today?' they could look it up from the till — or glance at the chalkboard where they wrote it five minutes ago. Historical prices (last month's latte) stay on the chalkboard for an hour because they never change. Today's price erases after five minutes in case the boss raised it. And while you're ordering, the barista is already making your drink before you've finished talking — that's the preloaded Task.
Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.suggested_intro_hook: 2000 milliseconds or 1 millisecond? That's the gap between 'database hit' and 'memory hit' for the same stock query in this system. Multiply that by a few hundred tab clicks per hour and you understand why the author built a decorator cache with time-graduated expiration.
key_takeaways: Decorator pattern lets you bolt caching onto a service without the service knowing it's being cached
Graduated cache expiration (long for immutable historical data, short for mutable recent data) gets the best of both worlds
Task preloading — assign StockService.GetCurrentStockAsync(id) to a field in OnInitializedAsync without awaiting it, then await it when the user actually needs it — makes tab clicks feel instant
Raw SQL function calls via DbConnection + SqlParameter sidestep EF Core for queries that are too complex or performance-critical for LINQ
IDbContextFactory + await using is the safe way to do concurrent DB work in Blazor Server without crashing the scoped DbContext
MemoryCache needs SizeLimit and CompactionPercentage set or it will eat all your RAM
Health checks that report cache hit/miss ratios give you a real-time quality signal beyond just 'is the service up?'
Education/Stock/PT/SistemaServiçoStockDo.quality_notes: Formal, dense technical documentation — more reference manual than tutorial. Includes architecture diagrams (ASCII art preserved poorly in extraction), sequence diagrams (Mermaid), decision matrices, API reference, troubleshooting table, and future improvement backlog. High signal density. Portuguese-language version of the Stock Service documentation — same system as the ENG variant.

Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.title: Sistema de Produção de Chão de Fábrica — Guia Para Totós (PT)
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.one_line_summary: Portuguese 'For Dummies' style walkthrough of the BioBraga Factory Floor production tracking system — explaining Factory_New.razor, MaterialConsumptionModal.razor, and FactoryFloorService.cs as a restaurant kitchen metaphor with a day-in-the-life worker scenario.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.executive_summary: A non-technical tour of the Factory Floor production tracking system described through the story of João the machine operator: he opens the page, selects his machine, clicks Start on an order, pauses for lunch (triggering the Material Consumption modal), and clicks Stop at the end. The doc teaches what each of the three main files does (the dashboard page, the material consumption modal, the service brain) using analogies to a restaurant kitchen order screen, a chef's prep sheet, and an efficient office manager. Explains smart features like historical-average material suggestions, automatic stock deduction, Primavera accounting integration, and PIN-gated actions without showing any code.
key_concepts: material consumption calculation from produced quantity

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Before this system, production was tracked on paper: workers would scribble quantities and material use on sheets that got lost, managers had no real-time visibility into production, stock counts were always wrong because nobody logged material consumption accurately, and accounting only learned about production at month-end. The system exists to digitize all of that: every production order start, pause, stop, and material confirmation is captured at the exact moment it happens, stock counts update automatically, and accounting gets the data instantly via Primavera integration.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides three coordinated pieces. Factory_New.razor is the shop-floor dashboard — shows today's stats (produced/remaining), a machine selector, and two columns of work orders (Por Iniciar / Iniciadas). Workers click Start/Pause/Stop on order cards. MaterialConsumptionModal.razor appears whenever a worker pauses or finishes an order — it collects units produced, waste count, and a table of materials consumed (pre-filled with calculated suggestions based on produced quantity and historical averages, with red warnings when stock is low). FactoryFloorService.cs is the invisible logic layer that marks orders in-progress, deducts materials from stock, adds finished goods to inventory, records waste, and pushes everything to Primavera accounting.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The day-in-the-life scenario: João arrives at 8:00, opens the system on a factory tablet, enters his PIN, selects Machine #3, and sees Order #1234 (make 100 plastic bottles). He clicks Start, enters his PIN, and the order moves from Por Iniciar to Iniciadas with a timestamp. At 12:00 he pauses for lunch — the material modal appears, he enters '60 bottles produced', the system suggests '6kg of plastic used' based on proportional calculation, he confirms, and the system atomically deducts 6kg from warehouse stock, adds 60 bottles to finished goods, updates the order to 40 remaining, and records the timestamp. After lunch he resumes, finishes the order at 14:30, clicks Stop, enters 40 produced and 2 waste, and the order marks Completa. Meanwhile Gestora Maria sees all of this live on her dashboard. Smart checks prevent impossible orders (not enough stock), prevent negative quantities, and require PIN on every significant action.

Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.suggested_metaphor: The Factory Floor system is a smart kitchen. Factory_New.razor is the order-ticket screen above the pass. The Material Consumption modal is the chef's prep sheet plus the 'what we actually used' tally. FactoryFloorService is the invisible sous chef who, the moment the ticket comes in, starts the timer, updates the mise en place count, and silently WhatsApps the accountant.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.suggested_intro_hook: What if the difference between 'making 50 bottles' and 'the company accountant knowing you made 50 bottles, updating the warehouse, and invoicing the customer' was one click from João with a smudged PIN?
key_takeaways: Digitizing shop-floor tracking moves production data from 'end-of-month guess' to 'live, accurate, per-action'
PIN gating on every Start/Pause/Stop action is the shop-floor equivalent of a time clock plus a signature
Smart material suggestions based on historical averages reduce data-entry friction while still letting workers override
One action in the UI (Confirm Production) triggers four downstream updates: stock deduction, finished-goods addition, waste log, and Primavera accounting push
Preventing impossible orders (not enough stock) at the UI layer is cheaper than rolling back a bad production run
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.quality_notes: Pure narrative doc — zero code snippets, deliberately so. The audience is plant managers or new hires, not developers. Effective at answering 'what does this system do?' without getting into implementation. Portuguese 'For Totós' variant — should pair with its technical counterpart when rendered.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.series_name: Factory Floor Documentation (PT Para Totós + ENG + Technical)

Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.title: Strategy Pattern in Export Services
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.one_line_summary: Walkthrough of the Strategy Pattern applied to a real AttendanceExportService using two-dimensional strategy injection: six IReportBuilder strategies (report type) crossed with three IExportGenerator strategies (output format) discovered via DI as IEnumerable<T>.
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.executive_summary: Uses a concrete Attendance Export Service to teach the Strategy Pattern and show how SRP, OCP, DIP, LSP, and ISP all emerge naturally from a good pattern implementation. The orchestrator (AttendanceExportService) receives IEnumerable<IReportBuilder> and IEnumerable<IExportGenerator> from DI, turns them into dictionaries keyed by type/format, and dispatches in O(1). Adding a new report type or format is zero changes to existing code — just register a new class in DI. Demonstrates the two-dimensional strategy matrix: 6 builders x 3 generators = 18 combinations but only 9 classes.
key_concepts: IEnumerable<T> injection in ASP.NET Core DI
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.suggested_metaphor: A strategy pattern with IEnumerable DI is like a buffet hot-table. The kitchen (DI container) keeps putting out pans labelled by what they contain — IReportBuilder:Attendance, IExportGenerator:Excel — and the orchestrator is the server with a ladle who just reads the label on your request ticket and scoops from the matching pan. Want to add a new dish? Drop a new pan on the table. The server never changes.
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.suggested_intro_hook: You're going to be asked for a new export format at 5pm on a Friday. If your answer involves touching a switch statement with 18 cases, you will still be here at 8pm. If your answer is 'new class, one DI registration, done', you'll make the 6pm tram. This doc is about buying yourself that tram.
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.what_it_teaches: How to refactor a 'giant switch statement' report generator into orthogonal strategy interfaces (IReportBuilder for WHAT data to build, IExportGenerator for HOW to output it), how to inject all implementations at once via IEnumerable<T> so new strategies auto-register, how dictionary-keyed dispatch gives O(1) lookup, why the identity property (ReportType / Format) must live on the interface so the orchestrator can build its dictionary, and how each SOLID principle shows up concretely: SRP (each class has one job), OCP (new report = new class, zero edits), DIP (orchestrator depends on interfaces not concrete types), LSP (any IReportBuilder can stand in for any other), ISP (two focused interfaces instead of one bloated one). Ends with xUnit test examples showing each strategy is testable in isolation.
key_takeaways: A strategy pattern separates WHAT to do (report type) from HOW to do it (output format) into orthogonal interfaces
Registering multiple implementations of the same interface lets DI inject them all as IEnumerable<T> — no manual factory needed
Putting an identity property (like ReportType ReportType { get; }) on the strategy interface lets the orchestrator build a Dictionary<TKey, TStrategy> for O(1) dispatch
Adding a new format is a new class + one AddTransient line — zero changes to the orchestrator
A two-dimensional strategy matrix (6 report types x 3 formats = 18 combos) takes only 9 classes instead of 18
Each strategy is testable in total isolation because it only depends on what its own interface contract requires
The orchestrator (AttendanceExportService) is the Context in GoF Strategy terminology — it owns the selection logic but delegates the actual work
Education/13-Export-Service-Strategy-Pat.quality_notes: Clean, well-structured doc. Good progression from bad example (giant switch) to good example (strategy + DI). Code examples are realistic and match the author's actual project. The 'two-dimensional strategy' section is a genuine insight. ASCII architecture diagram is clear.

Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.title: How To Create Unit Testing — xUnit + EF Core InMemory Setup Guide
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.one_line_summary: Nine-step copy-pasteable guide to bootstrapping an xUnit test project for an ASP.NET Core + EF Core MVC app, using Moq, FluentAssertions, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory, and a per-test ApplicationDbContext factory.
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.executive_summary: A concrete command-by-command tutorial to stand up the SambientalMVC.Tests project alongside a main MVC app: dotnet new xunit, solution add, reference add, NuGet packages, GlobalUsings.cs, a TestDbContextFactory with Guid-based InMemoryDatabase isolation, then three sample test classes (AgendaMaintenanceServiceTests, RecurringServiceProcessorTests, AgendaHostedServiceTests) demonstrating arrange-act-assert, IDisposable-based cleanup, and a BackgroundService test harness. Ends with dotnet test invocation patterns.
key_concepts: DbContext test factory with Guid-named databases
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.suggested_metaphor: Bootstrapping a unit test project is like setting up a crash-test dummy lab for your code. Each test is a crash: you strap in an Arrange, hit the wall with an Act, then inspect the dented fender with an Assert. The InMemory database is the foam-padded test car — looks real, behaves real enough, and you can throw it away between crashes.
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.suggested_intro_hook: Your PR reviewer just said 'add tests'. You open Google, you get 40 blog posts and 6 different frameworks. This is the nine commands you actually needed — in order.
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.what_it_teaches: How to add a test project to an existing ASP.NET Core + EF Core solution without wrestling with configuration. Covers the exact CLI invocations (dotnet new xunit, dotnet sln add, dotnet add reference, dotnet add package for EFCore.InMemory/Moq/FluentAssertions/Mvc.Testing), the GlobalUsings.cs trick to avoid repeated namespace imports, a per-test unique-database TestDbContextFactory (Guid.NewGuid().ToString() as database name to prevent test pollution), the IDisposable pattern for context cleanup between tests, AAA test structure with FluentAssertions, and a working example of testing an IHostedService/BackgroundService by building a custom ServiceCollection test harness and running it with a CancellationToken.
key_takeaways: dotnet new xunit + dotnet sln add + dotnet add reference is the three-command path from nothing to a wired-up test project
Use Guid.NewGuid().ToString() as the InMemory database name so every test gets a clean isolated DB — no cross-test pollution
GlobalUsings.cs (global using Xunit; global using FluentAssertions; etc.) eliminates the repeated import boilerplate in every test file
IDisposable on the test class is the canonical cleanup hook — xUnit creates a new test class instance per test, so ctor = setup and Dispose = teardown
Testing a BackgroundService works by building a mini ServiceCollection in the test, resolving the service, calling StartAsync with a short-timeout CancellationToken, and asserting on the DB state
FluentAssertions (.Should().Be(), .Should().HaveCount(1)) reads like English and produces much better failure messages than plain Assert.Equal
Microsoft_Fullstack/HowToCreateUnitTesti.quality_notes: Functional step-by-step, light on theory. Reads like copy-paste snippets the author kept for personal reference — which is fine for its purpose. Uses real project names (SambientalMVC, AgendaMaintenanceService, AgendaRecorrente) so probably extracted from a specific project's onboarding docs. DOCX extraction preserved code blocks reasonably.

Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.title: Static Events Problem — The Shared Loudspeaker Bug (For Dummies)
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.one_line_summary: A one-page analogy explaining the static-event cross-user leakage bug in a multi-kiosk Blazor Server facial recognition app: a single static event acted like a loudspeaker broadcasting every user's identification to every other kiosk, fixed by per-kiosk instance IDs acting as private mailboxes.
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.executive_summary: The companion 'For Dummies' doc for a technical static-events writeup. Explains with ASCII diagrams why two facial-recognition kiosks were seeing each other's user identifications: the C# static event was a shared loudspeaker — when Alice's kiosk fired 'Face detected!', Bob's kiosk also received it because static events are process-global. The fix was to include a unique instance ID on each event and filter on the receiving side, turning the loudspeaker into per-instance private mailboxes.
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.suggested_metaphor: A static event is the office loudspeaker. If the front desk pages 'John, your package!' over it, every cubicle hears it — including John in cubicle A AND Jane in cubicle B who's now looking at John's name on her screen. The fix is to stop paging and start handing out addressed envelopes.
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.suggested_intro_hook: Alice scanned her face at Kiosk A. Bob was standing at Kiosk B and suddenly saw 'Welcome, Alice!' on his screen. The bug wasn't facial recognition — it was one word in the event declaration: static.
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.what_it_teaches: Why static events in a multi-user Blazor Server app are dangerous: they live at the process level, so every active circuit (user session) receives every event firing. Shows with before/after ASCII diagrams how a 'shared loudspeaker' bug leaks one user's data to every other user, and how giving each component instance a unique ID and filtering events on that ID turns it into a 'private mailbox' per user. The doc intentionally avoids code — it's the gentle explainer that pairs with a technical companion doc.
key_takeaways: Static events in Blazor Server are process-global, so they broadcast to every active user circuit simultaneously
A shared event with no correlation ID will leak one user's data to every other user on the same server instance
The fix is per-instance identity: each component generates a unique ID, includes it with the event, and filters on the receiving side
Analogy rule of thumb: when multiple users might do the same thing at the same time, each user needs their own private channel — not a shared broadcast
This is the Blazor Server equivalent of the classic 'static member holds request-scoped data' bug in ASP.NET
Education/ForDummies/06-Blazor-JS-Intero.quality_notes: Very short (~400 words) but focused. Effective at conveying the core bug without any code. Explicitly references its technical companion at the bottom, confirming it's part of a paired doc set. Belongs to a numbered ForDummies track (06-).

Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.title: Stack and Heap in C# — Understanding Memory Management in .NET
Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.one_line_summary: A comprehensive tour of .NET memory management covering stack vs heap, value vs reference types, boxing, garbage collection, leaks, and performance optimization techniques.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.executive_summary: This guide walks from the history of manual memory management through the CLR's managed model, explaining why value types usually live on the stack while reference types live on the managed heap and references themselves are 8 bytes regardless of object size. It then dives into GC generations, the mark-sweep-compact algorithm, boxing/unboxing costs, stack allocation with stackalloc, and subtle cases like strings, captured closures, and struct fields inside classes. The second half is practical: identifying memory leaks (events, static caches, captured variables, Blazor circuits), reducing allocations with ArrayPool and Span<T>, avoiding the Large Object Heap, and using IDisposable correctly. The key insight is that managed memory isn't free — understanding where data lives lets you write code that cooperates with the GC instead of fighting it.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.suggested_metaphor: Think of the stack as your kitchen counter and the heap as your garage. The counter is tiny but you can grab things instantly, and whenever you finish a recipe you wipe it clean without thinking. The garage is huge, but finding something takes a walk, and someone has to occasionally come through and sweep up the boxes nobody's using anymore — that someone is the garbage collector.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.suggested_intro_hook: Your C# code has never had a memory leak... or has it? The garbage collector protects you from forgetting to call free(), but it can't save you from an event handler that silently keeps a 100MB object alive for the rest of the app's life. Understanding what lives where is the difference between 'my app works' and 'my app works at scale'.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Stack_and_Heap_G.what_it_teaches: How .NET's memory model actually works under the covers — which data lives on the stack vs the heap, how generational GC decides what to collect and when, how boxing silently allocates objects, where .NET apps still leak memory despite having a GC, and what tools and techniques (pooling, Span<T>, stackalloc, pre-sizing, proper Dispose) actually move the needle on performance.
key_takeaways: Value types live on the stack by default but move to the heap when they're fields of a class, array elements, boxed, or captured by a closure
A reference is always 8 bytes on 64-bit; the object it points to can be anywhere from 16 bytes to gigabytes on the heap
The GC is generational because most objects die young — Gen0 collections are cheap, Gen2 collections hurt
Boxing is a silent performance killer: ArrayList.Add(int) allocates on every call, List<int>.Add(int) does not
.NET memory leaks are almost always event handlers, static collections, long-lived delegates with captured state, or un-disposed Blazor subscriptions
Reaching for ArrayPool, Span<T>, stackalloc, and pre-sized collections is how you drop allocation counts in hot paths

Education/Educational_ML/neural-network-.one_line_summary: An interactive, zero-math-required tutorial that builds a neural network from first principles through the lens of a 20 Questions game that learns which animal you're thinking of.
Education/Educational_ML/neural-network-.executive_summary: This is a guided, 17-slide educational journey that explains neural networks without assuming any background beyond basic arithmetic. It starts by turning animals into feature vectors, compares them with k-Nearest Neighbors distance, then shows why that fails when two animals have identical features — motivating the need for learning. From there it introduces a single artificial neuron (multiply inputs by weights, add, squash through sigmoid), walks through the weight update rule, extends to one-neuron-per-class, exposes the XOR limitation to motivate hidden layers, and finally arrives at backpropagation using the soccer-team analogy to explain credit assignment. The companion project is a C# + Blazor implementation called TwentyQ, so this doc is the conceptual foundation that lets a .NET developer understand why they're writing the code they're writing.
Education/Educational_ML/neural-network-.suggested_metaphor: A neural network learns the way a toddler learns 'dog': nobody hands them a rulebook saying 'four legs AND fur AND barks'. Instead they see hundreds of dogs, some poodles and some great danes, and the pattern slowly etches itself into their brain. The weights in a neuron are exactly that etching — they start random and get nudged every time the network is wrong, until the bumps and grooves happen to match the shape of 'dog-ness'.
Education/Educational_ML/neural-network-.suggested_intro_hook: Everyone uses AI. Almost nobody can explain, in plain English, what a 'weight' actually is. If you can explain a weight and a sigmoid to a curious twelve-year-old, you're already in the top 1% of people who talk about machine learning.
Education/Educational_ML/neural-network-.what_it_teaches: How a neural network actually works — not as a magic black box but as a chain of very simple arithmetic operations (multiply, add, squash) whose numbers get nudged by a recipe called gradient descent until the output starts matching what you wanted. The doc covers why single neurons can't solve XOR, why hidden layers fix that by learning intermediate features, and how backpropagation distributes blame through the network so every weight knows which direction to move.
key_takeaways: Classification is the core shape of most ML: turn stuff into numbers, then decide which category those numbers belong to
A neuron is just 'multiply inputs by weights, add them up, squash the result' — nothing magical
Learning is a loop: predict, measure error, nudge weights, repeat. The learning rate controls how big the nudges are
A single-layer network can only separate data with a straight line — XOR proves why you need hidden layers
Backpropagation distributes blame proportional to how strongly each neuron contributed to the output, using the exact same weights that carried signals forward
The sigmoid derivative makes confident neurons learn slowly — which is why the network doesn't forget what it already knows

Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.title: Expression Trees & Compiled Reflection — From Slow Reflection to Native Speed
Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.one_line_summary: How to build a ReflectionCache that compiles property getters and setters into delegates at runtime so config-driven property access runs at native speed instead of 100x slower reflection.
Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.executive_summary: The doc tackles a real problem: when a config file names properties as strings, the naive solution is PropertyInfo.GetValue, which is roughly 100x slower than direct access because each call re-looks up metadata and boxes values. It walks through building an expression tree — Parameter → Convert → Property → Convert → Lambda → Compile — to produce a native delegate equivalent to hand-written code, then caches the delegate in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by (Type, propertyName) so compilation only happens once per pair. The critical distinction it hammers home is Expression<Func<T,R>> (data, inspectable, what EF Core translates to SQL) versus Func<T,R> (already-compiled machine code), because passing a compiled Func to EF Core's Where collapses server-side filtering into client-side evaluation — a catastrophe this doc helps you avoid.
Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.suggested_metaphor: Reflection is like opening the cookbook every single time you need to chop an onion — you re-read which page, re-read the technique, then finally cut. A compiled expression is what happens after you've made that recipe fifty times: your hands just know. You pay for studying once; after that, every onion gets chopped at muscle-memory speed.
Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.suggested_intro_hook: Your config file says 'CodeProperty: Codigo' and suddenly you're calling PropertyInfo.GetValue 50,000 times per page load. The profiler lights up red. You need dynamic property access without the dynamic tax — and .NET has a trick for that, hiding in the System.Linq.Expressions namespace.
Education/26-Expression-Trees-Compiled-R.what_it_teaches: How to build, compile, and cache expression trees so that config-driven or generic property access runs essentially as fast as hand-written code. It also teaches the crucial distinction between an expression tree (inspectable data) and a compiled delegate (executable code) — the same distinction that determines whether EF Core generates SQL or materializes the entire table.
key_takeaways: PropertyInfo.GetValue is about 100x slower than direct access; compiled expressions are within 3x
Build the tree once with Expression.Parameter → Convert → Property → Convert → Lambda → Compile
Cache the resulting delegate in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by (Type, propertyName) — use GetOrAdd so two threads racing the same key is harmless
Expression<Func<T,R>> is data; Func<T,R> is compiled code. Pass the wrong one to EF Core and you pull the whole table into memory
Use compiled expressions for repeated config-driven property access; use raw PropertyInfo for one-off lookups; use direct access when you know the property at compile time

Includes a metaphor of its own (cookbook) and the three-layer navigation analogy. Part of a numbered tutorial series (#26).

Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.title: Stock Service System — Formal Technical Documentation
Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.one_line_summary: Formal technical reference for a high-performance inventory tracking system built around a decorator-pattern cached service layer, SQL Server functions, pre-loading tasks, and graduated cache expiration.
Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.executive_summary: This is the formal architecture document for the Stock Service — a three-layer system (UI/Service/Data) where a CachedStockService decorator wraps a StockService implementation that talks to SQL Server table-valued functions (fn_ArtigoStockByDate, fn_ArtigoUsedInFluxo) through a raw ADO.NET connection for performance. The caching strategy uses graduated expiration: 1 hour for historical data older than 7 days, 5 minutes for recent data, nothing at all for filtered queries. Razor components pre-load expensive operations as Tasks in OnInitializedAsync so that by the time the user clicks the Stock tab, the data is already there. The doc also covers extension methods, health checks, structured logging with cache-hit tagging, cache inspection endpoints, and future enhancements like Redis and SignalR-driven invalidation.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Inventory queries are the most asked question in a warehouse ERP, and they're brutally expensive because computing 'what did I have on January 15th?' means summing every movement from the beginning of time up to that date. Hitting the database for every query brings the system to its knees and users wait 2-3 seconds every single time. The Stock Service exists to eliminate that wait by caching aggressively for data that doesn't change (historical stock) and conservatively for data that might (today's stock), while never caching filtered queries that are too specific to repeat. The result is sub-millisecond responses for 99% of queries with the database staying cool.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Exposes an IStockService with four operations: GetArticleStockByDateAsync (point-in-time query), GetStockMovementsAsync (movement history with optional date filters), GetStockTotalsAsync (aggregate entradas/saídas), and CheckFluxoAsync (per-document-line flow). A CachedStockService wraps the real StockService as a decorator and checks IMemoryCache first, falling back to the real service on miss and then storing the result with an expiration chosen based on how old the queried date is. The UI layer (ArtigoDetalhe.razor) kicks off stock queries as Tasks in OnInitializedAsync so that clicking the Stock tab awaits an already-completed task.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Under the hood, the StockService opens a raw SqlCommand on the DbContext's connection and invokes the dbo.fn_ArtigoStockByDate table-valued function with parameterized arguments — deliberately bypassing EF Core's change tracker and LINQ translation for maximum speed. A 'smart trick' adds one day to the filter date so the query includes everything up to end-of-day. Movement queries use EF Core LINQ with three joins (CrmDocumentoDetalhes → CrmDocumentos → CrmTipoDocumentos → CrmSerieDocumentos) filtered by Movstocks=true. The CachedStockService generates keys like 'stock_{artigoId}_{yyyyMMdd}' and picks an expiration: TimeSpan.FromHours(1) if the date is more than 7 days old, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) otherwise. The Razor layer orchestrates task reuse — if a filter hasn't changed, it awaits the existing _stockMovementsTask field; if the filter did change, it creates a new task and parallel-awaits a totals task alongside it. Health checks run a test query + cache statistics, and structured logging emits one-line entries with ArticleId, Date, CacheHit, and ExecutionTime tags for monitoring.

Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.suggested_metaphor: The Stock Service is a coffee shop with a secret second menu — the barista keeps sticky notes of the most recent orders so that if you ask for the same drink someone just ordered, they hand it to you instantly. Regular espresso from yesterday? Sticky note lasts an hour because yesterday can't change. Today's cappuccino? Sticky note lasts five minutes because someone might modify it. A custom half-caf oat milk with exactly 1.5 pumps of vanilla? No sticky note — too specific, nobody else is ordering that.
Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.suggested_intro_hook: Every time a user clicks the Stock tab on an article page, the database has to sum every inbound and outbound movement since the beginning of time to tell them how many units are on the shelf. That's expensive. Now imagine 40 users clicking that tab every minute across 50,000 articles. This is how you make that scream instead of crawl.
Education/Stock/ENG/StockServiceSystemFo.what_it_teaches: How to architect a read-heavy service in .NET using the decorator pattern, graduated in-memory caching, SQL Server table-valued functions for aggregation performance, and Blazor task pre-loading to make the UI feel instant even on slow queries.
key_takeaways: Wrap expensive services with a cached decorator so caching logic lives in one place and tests can swap it out
Cache expiration should be proportional to how likely the data is to change — historical = long, recent = short, filtered = don't bother
SQL Server table-valued functions called via raw ADO.NET skip EF Core overhead and are perfect for pure-aggregate queries
Start expensive Tasks in OnInitializedAsync and store them as fields — clicking a tab then awaits an already-complete task
Cache keys should encode everything that distinguishes the query (artigoId + date) and the format should be predictable for manual invalidation
Monitor cache hit rates via IMemoryCache.GetCurrentStatistics in a health check — if the ratio degrades, something upstream changed

Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.title: Blazor JS Interop — Static Events vs Instance-Isolated Callbacks
Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.one_line_summary: Why static C# events in Blazor JS interop leak data between concurrent component instances, and how to fix it with a ConcurrentDictionary of per-instance callbacks keyed by Guid.
Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.executive_summary: The doc walks through a real, ugly bug: two facial recognition kiosks running simultaneously were subscribed to the same static event (FacialRecognitionHelper.OnFacialIdentifyComplete), so when Alice scanned her face at Kiosk A, both kiosks received the event and displayed 'Welcome Alice!' — then seconds later Bob scanned at Kiosk B and both screens switched to 'Welcome Bob!'. The fix is instance-isolated callbacks: each component generates a Guid instanceId in OnInitialized, registers a callback in a static ConcurrentDictionary<string, Action<string>>, passes that instanceId through to JavaScript when starting the capture, and unregisters in Dispose(). The JSInvokable method now takes instanceId as its first parameter and only invokes the matching callback. The doc is careful to note that static events are still fine for truly app-level notifications — the rule is 'if more than one instance can exist, route by instanceId'.
Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.suggested_metaphor: A static event in Blazor JS interop is like announcing 'pizza's here!' over an entire office PA system — every team on every floor hears it, and if two teams ordered pizza at the same time, you end up with everyone running to the wrong lobby. Instance-isolated callbacks are like texting the specific person who ordered it. The message goes exactly where it needs to, and nobody else's lunch gets interrupted.
Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.suggested_intro_hook: You ship a facial recognition kiosk. The demo goes great with one user. Then you deploy a second kiosk in the lobby downstairs, and suddenly when someone scans their face, the wrong person's name shows up on the wrong screen. The bug lives in a single C# keyword you probably didn't think twice about: `static`.
Education/06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Ev.what_it_teaches: Why static C# events in Blazor JS interop broadcast to every subscriber and how that silently breaks multi-instance scenarios. The fix: each component registers itself in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by a Guid, passes that Guid down to JavaScript, and the JSInvokable method routes the callback back only to the specific instance that initiated the action. Also covers when static events are still acceptable (truly app-level broadcasts).
key_takeaways: Static events broadcast — every subscriber receives every event, which is almost never what you want for user-specific data
Give each component instance a Guid and register it in a static ConcurrentDictionary<string, Action<T>>
Pass the instanceId through JavaScript all the way to the [JSInvokable] method so callbacks route to the right instance
ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe without explicit locks — perfect for this pattern
Always unregister in Dispose() to prevent memory leaks from lingering callback references
Static events are still OK when only one instance will ever exist OR when the notification is genuinely app-level
