Education/07-Facial-Recognition-Architec.one_line_summary: Architecture document for HRModule's facial-recognition attendance system: face-api.js runs ML models in the browser to extract a 128-dimensional descriptor, which the Blazor server matches against stored biomarkers via Euclidean distance.
Education/07-Facial-Recognition-Architec.executive_summary: The system is a hybrid client-server design: the browser owns all the heavy ML (face detection, landmark extraction, 128-dim descriptor generation via face-api.js), while the C# server only sees mathematical vectors and makes the final authentication decision. This split is important for three reasons — privacy (raw images never leave the device), performance (no video streaming), and security (descriptors are irreversible). The server side routes JSInvokable callbacks through a static FacialRecognitionHelper to per-component instances, then delegates to an orchestrator that discovers the employee's tenant database and calls FacialRecognitionService.IdentifyForAttendanceAsync, which loads all user biomarkers and returns the best match by Euclidean distance below a 0.5 threshold. Ten consecutive detections are required before the descriptor is sent — a cheap but effective anti-spoofing layer.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Employees need to check in and out without fumbling for cards, remembering passwords, or typing on a greasy factory tablet. Facial recognition solves all three — it's contactless, always available, and fast. But uploading webcam video to a server is a privacy, bandwidth, and performance disaster, so the system is designed so the heavy ML runs in the browser and only a mathematical fingerprint crosses the wire.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: A user looks into the camera on a kiosk or their own device. The browser runs face detection, landmark extraction, and descriptor generation (128 floats). After 10 consecutive stable detections (anti-spoofing), the descriptor is sent to the Blazor server via a JSInvokable callback. The server looks up the employee's tenant database, loads all users' stored biomarkers, and finds the closest match by Euclidean distance. If the distance is under 0.5, it's a match — the UI then shows the employee and offers CheckIn / CheckOut / Break buttons. If over 0.5, no match.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The browser side is face-api.js + a custom script.js that runs a setInterval loop calling detectSingleFace().withFaceLandmarks().withFaceDescriptor(). When score >= 0.5 for 10 consecutive frames, it calls DotNet.invokeMethodAsync('NotifyFacialIdentifyCompleteForInstance', instanceId, descriptor). The server side has a static FacialRecognitionHelper with a concurrent dictionary of instanceId -> callback, so multiple simultaneous kiosk components can coexist. The callback resolves to a FacialAttendanceComponent method, which hands off to FacialAttendanceOrchestrator. The orchestrator discovers the employee's company database (multi-tenant), then calls FacialRecognitionService.IdentifyForAttendanceAsync, which loads all CrmUtilizador rows with non-null Biomarkers and iterates, computing sum of squared differences across 128 dimensions, then returns the best match if below the configured threshold (default 0.5 from appsettings.json). The resulting UserId flows back to the UI, which shows name/status and offers action buttons. Actions call AttendanceService.CheckInAsync/CheckOutAsync/etc, which record the entry with GPS and timestamps.

Education/07-Facial-Recognition-Architec.suggested_metaphor: Your face becomes 128 numbers — think of it as your geometric fingerprint. The browser is a math tutor that stares at you and writes those numbers on a napkin. The napkin travels to the server, which has a binder full of everyone else's napkins and does a 128-dimensional game of 'one of these is not like the others' until it finds yours. And because napkins can't be reversed back into faces, it doesn't matter if someone intercepts one — it's like trying to rebuild a person from their height and blood pressure.
Education/07-Facial-Recognition-Architec.suggested_intro_hook: Streaming video to a server for face recognition is the wrong architecture — it's slow, it's bandwidth-heavy, and it's terrible for privacy. The right architecture is to never let the video leave the device at all. Only 512 bytes of math cross the wire, and that math can't be reversed into a face. Here's how the HRModule does it.
key_takeaways: Run ML in the browser when you can — face-api.js keeps raw imagery on-device and only sends a 128-float descriptor
Use a static dictionary keyed by instanceId to route JSInvokable callbacks back to specific component instances
Euclidean distance in descriptor space = similarity; a threshold of ~0.5 is a good starting balance
Require N consecutive detections before trusting a result — cheap anti-spoofing against held-up photos
Descriptors are one-way — you can't reconstruct a face from them, so they're safer to transmit than images
Server must still be the sole authority on identity — the client only reports observations, it doesn't authenticate
Education/07-Facial-Recognition-Architec.quality_notes: Strong architecture document with a clear client/server split diagram, data flow example, security reasoning, and a full file manifest. Code samples are concise and on-point. Missing: latency numbers, what happens when two people look at the camera at once, how biomarkers are enrolled in the first place.

Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.title: Facial Recognition - For Dummies
Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.one_line_summary: A plain-language explainer of the facial recognition attendance system that shows how a face becomes 128 numbers, how those numbers are matched against a 'phonebook' of known faces, and why only the numbers — never the photo — leave the device.
Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.executive_summary: This is the non-technical companion to the HRModule facial recognition architecture doc. It explains the same system in four friendly steps: phone sees your face, ML turns it into 128 numbers, server compares those numbers against the 'face phonebook,' and if there's a match it welcomes you. It also covers why 10 consecutive detections are required (so a photo doesn't work) and the privacy story (numbers can't be reversed into a face — like knowing someone's height and weight doesn't let you draw them).

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Because the engineering architecture doc is dense and uses words like 'JSInvokable,' 'Euclidean distance,' and 'descriptor' — which is fine for developers but useless for anyone who just wants to understand how the login kiosk knows who they are. This version exists so a manager, a new hire, or a curious employee can grasp the system in five minutes without touching any code.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Walks the reader through the four-step flow of a facial check-in — camera sees face, math turns face into 128 numbers, server compares numbers to stored ones, welcome message — and answers the two most common questions non-technical people have: 'is someone storing my photo?' and 'can I fool it with a picture?'
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: It leans on analogies: face-to-numbers is like a fingerprint, server comparison is like a phonebook lookup, the 10-detection requirement is like needing to confirm a password twice, and the privacy explanation is 'knowing someone's height and weight doesn't let you draw them.' The visual flow is shown with ASCII art of a camera, a face emoji, a progress bar, and a welcome screen. There is no code — just concepts, emojis, and simple diagrams.

Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.suggested_metaphor: Your face has 128 secret measurements — the distance between your eyes, how wide your jaw is, where your mouth sits. The camera reads those measurements and scribbles them on a slip of paper. The slip goes to the server, which has a filing cabinet of everyone's slips. It flips through until it finds one that matches yours. And the slip? You couldn't draw a face from it any more than you could draw me from my height and weight.
Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.suggested_intro_hook: When you look at a kiosk camera and it says 'Welcome, João' two seconds later, you might think your photo is sitting on a server somewhere. It isn't. What's actually on the server is 128 little numbers — and those numbers can't be turned back into a face, no matter how hard anyone tries.
key_takeaways: Your face becomes 128 numerical measurements — like a mathematical fingerprint
Only the numbers are sent to the server, never your actual photo
The server compares your numbers to the stored numbers of known employees
10 consecutive checks are required so a held-up photo can't fool the system
Numbers cannot be reversed into a face, so they're safe to transmit
Education/ForDummies/07-Facial-Recogniti.quality_notes: Concise, friendly, very clear. Exactly what 'for dummies' should be — short, analogical, visual, no jargon. Perfect as a handout for non-engineering staff or a footer link from the technical doc.

Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.title: Backpropagation Visualized
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.one_line_summary: An interactive SVG-based visualization of a tiny neural network (6 inputs → 6 hidden → 8 outputs) walking through the four stages of backpropagation: forward pass, output errors, error propagation backward, and weight update.
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.executive_summary: This is a self-contained interactive HTML page that visualizes how a feedforward neural network classifies animals from 6 binary-ish inputs (Fly? Swim? Mammal? Bird? Feline? Danger?) and learns from mistakes via backpropagation. The user clicks four buttons to step through: (1) forward pass — data flows left-to-right and each neuron computes sigmoid(Σ weighted inputs); (2) output errors — compare predictions to expected and color-code the gap; (3) backpropagation — highlight the error flowing backward through the hidden layer; (4) weight update — show which weights get nudged. It's intentionally pedagogical, not a library — the aim is intuition, not accuracy.
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.suggested_metaphor: Imagine a classroom where 6 students whisper answers to 6 teachers in the middle row, who then whisper to 8 judges at the back. The judges raise paddles with their guess. If the judges are wrong, the 'correction' whisper runs in reverse — each judge tells the middle teachers 'you nudged me the wrong way,' and the middle teachers tell the students 'you fed me bad info.' The next round, everyone whispers slightly differently. That's backpropagation — a chain of 'who's partially to blame?' running backward through the network.
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.suggested_intro_hook: Neural networks don't learn by magic — they learn by getting things wrong and then distributing the blame backward through every weight that contributed to the wrong answer. Most explanations of backprop are a wall of chain-rule calculus. Here's one with circles, arrows, and a button labeled '1. Forward Pass' — press it and watch the math light up.
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.what_it_teaches: How a small feedforward neural network processes inputs, generates outputs, measures how wrong the outputs are, propagates that error backward through the hidden layer, and uses that to update weights. It's designed to build intuition by animation rather than by formulas — you see the data flow, you see the errors, you see which connections are implicated.
key_takeaways: Forward pass flows left to right; backpropagation flows right to left
Error at an output = expected − actual; positive means predicted too low, negative means too high
Error propagates backward in proportion to the weights on the forward connections
Weight updates happen last, using the backpropagated error signal at each neuron
A network this small (6→6→8) is enough to visualize every step of the algorithm without clutter
Education/Educational_ML/backprop-visual.quality_notes: The extracted text file only captures page labels (buttons + title) because the actual educational content is rendered dynamically by JavaScript into SVG. The HTML source itself has layer structure, sample data (Cat: [0,0,2,0,2,0] → expected Cat index 4), and explanation text injected per-step. Great as an interactive supplement but useless as reading material without the live page. Ideal to embed in the webbook as an iframe so users can click through the steps.

Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.title: Generics in C#: A Comprehensive Guide
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.one_line_summary: A full historical and practical walkthrough of C# generics: why they exist, how constraints and variance work, and how reified generics differ from Java's erasure.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.executive_summary: This guide traces C# generics from the pre-generic dark ages (ArrayList with boxing and runtime casts) to modern patterns like Result<T>, IRepository<T>, and generic Blazor components. It covers syntax for generic classes, methods, structs, and interfaces; every kind of constraint (class, struct, new(), base class, interface, notnull, unmanaged); covariance and contravariance with the in/out keywords; and the critical CLR distinction that C# reifies generic type information at runtime while Java erases it. The document closes with best-practice patterns (Repository, Factory, Specification, Result/Either) and a tour of generics across EF Core, DI, and Blazor.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.suggested_metaphor: Generics are like a cookie cutter with a slot where you write the dough's name. The shape (List, Dictionary, Repository) is fixed, but you snap in 'int' or 'Employee' and the compiler stamps out a perfectly type-safe batch. Java's cutter has the name rubbed off by the time it hits the oven — C# keeps the label so the kitchen staff (the CLR) always knows what they baked.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.suggested_intro_hook: In 2003, if you wanted a type-safe list of integers in C#, you either wrote IntegerList from scratch or you used ArrayList and prayed nobody stuffed a string in there. Then C# 2.0 arrived, and one angle bracket changed everything.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.what_it_teaches: How to write, constrain, and consume generic types in C#; when to use each constraint; when variance is safe and how to express it with in/out; how the CLR's reified generics enable reflection tricks impossible in Java; and how canonical patterns like Repository, Factory, and Specification naturally shape themselves around generics.
key_takeaways: Generics eliminate the old dilemma between code reuse (object-based collections) and type safety (hand-rolled per-type classes)
Constraints are a contract: they let the compiler trust that T supports specific operations
Covariance (out) is safe only when T is produced; contravariance (in) is safe only when T is consumed
C# generics are reified — type arguments survive compilation and are queryable via reflection
Static fields on a generic type are per-constructed-type, not shared across Counter<int> and Counter<string>
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.m.quality_notes: Excellent long-form reference. Well-structured into seven parts with clear progression from history to advanced topics. Every concept has working code. A strong candidate to be the canonical generics chapter in the library.

Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.title: Strategy Pattern: Pluggable Algorithms
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.one_line_summary: The Strategy Pattern swaps an if/else algorithm chain for a set of interchangeable classes that all implement the same interface, selected at runtime by a key.
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.executive_summary: This tutorial teaches the Strategy Pattern by showing a concrete refactor: a 300-line DetectConflicts method with nested if/else on entityType becomes a small IScheduleConflictStrategy interface and two classes (EmployeeScheduleConflictStrategy, EquipmentScheduleConflictStrategy) that the ScheduleConflictDetector routes between using IEnumerable<IStrategy> injected by DI. It then generalises the pattern with additional real examples (IExportGenerator, IReportBuilder) and contrasts it with Chain of Responsibility, which runs all handlers in sequence rather than selecting one.
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.suggested_metaphor: The Strategy Pattern is like a universal power adapter: the wall (router) doesn't care whether you plug in a UK, US, or EU head — it just exposes the same socket and lets the adapter handle the voltage difference. Plug in a new country? Buy a new head, no rewiring the wall.
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.suggested_intro_hook: Every time you catch yourself writing 'if entityType == Employee do this, else if Equipment do that', a 300-line method is trying to be born. This tutorial shows you how to strangle it in the crib.
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.what_it_teaches: How to recognise the if/else-on-type smell, extract each branch into its own class behind a shared interface, and let .NET DI's IEnumerable<T> resolution act as your strategy registry. Also how to add new strategies (e.g., VehicleScheduleConflictStrategy) without touching a single line of existing code.
key_takeaways: Registering multiple implementations of the same interface makes DI double as a strategy registry
Each strategy self-declares its key via an EntityType/Format/ReportType property — the router never needs a switch
The router contains zero business logic: it is pure dispatch
Strategy selects ONE algorithm; Chain of Responsibility runs ALL of them — same wiring, opposite semantics
Open/Closed in action: adding VehicleStrategy requires one AddScoped line and zero existing-code edits
Education/31-Strategy-Pattern-Pluggable-.quality_notes: Strong tutorial with extensive real code from the GivingCare codebase. The comparison to Chain of Responsibility in Section 8 is a highlight — it distinguishes two patterns that often get confused. Labelled 'Tutorial #31' so clearly part of a numbered series.

Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.title: SemaphoreSlim: Controlled Access and Async Locking
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.one_line_summary: SemaphoreSlim is the async-friendly lock primitive you must use whenever your critical section contains an await — a role lock() fundamentally cannot fill.
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.executive_summary: This tutorial explains why the C# lock statement cannot contain await (because lock is thread-affine and await can resume on a different thread), and shows how SemaphoreSlim(1,1) replaces it as an async-safe mutex while SemaphoreSlim(N,N) doubles as a rate limiter for things like external API calls, PDF generation pools, and bulk DB operations. It walks through a real race condition in GivingCare's GlobalChatService.InitializeAsync, shows the WaitAsync/try-finally/Release pattern, covers timeouts and cancellation, and closes with a decision tree for picking between lock, SemaphoreSlim, ConcurrentDictionary, and no synchronisation at all.
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.suggested_metaphor: SemaphoreSlim is a parking garage with exactly N spots. WaitAsync() pulls up to the entrance and either drives in (spot available) or idles outside until one frees up — crucially, your engine isn't running while you wait (async, not blocking). Release() is backing out. Forget to back out once and that spot is lost forever; forget twice and the whole garage quietly seals itself shut.
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.suggested_intro_hook: You wrote lock(obj) { await DoWork(); }, the compiler screamed CS1996, and you 'fixed' it by moving the await just outside the brace. Congratulations — you just built a race condition with extra steps.
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.what_it_teaches: Why lock() refuses to mix with await, how SemaphoreSlim replaces it for both mutex and N-way throttling scenarios, the mandatory try/finally Release pattern, the subtle bug of releasing after a timed-out WaitAsync, and when NOT to use SemaphoreSlim (prefer ConcurrentDictionary, immutable data, or no sync at all).
key_takeaways: lock() cannot contain await because it tracks owning-thread identity; await can resume on a different thread
SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is the async mutex; SemaphoreSlim(N,N) is a concurrent-permit gate
Release() must live in a finally block — miss once and the semaphore deadlocks forever
Only Release() if WaitAsync actually returned true (important when using timeout overloads)
If you don't share state or you use ConcurrentDictionary, you don't need a semaphore at all
Education/30-SemaphoreSlim-Controlled-Ac.quality_notes: Excellent tutorial with a concrete GivingCare bug (GlobalChatService race) grounding the theory. The 'decision tree' at the end and the quick reference card are particularly strong. Tutorial #30 of a numbered series.

Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.title: SignalR Real-Time Chat System
Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.one_line_summary: A walkthrough of the GivingCare chat module: a four-layer SignalR architecture (ChatHub, ChatService, GlobalChatService, UI) with multi-device online tracking, read receipts, typing indicators, and per-company feature flag gating.
Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.executive_summary: This document explains the chat system implemented in GivingCare 3.0: how the layers (UI, GlobalChatService client wrapper, ChatHub, ChatService, EF Core) cooperate; how a ConcurrentDictionary<int, HashSet<string>> maps one user to many device connections for correct online/offline broadcasts; the ServiceResult pattern used for all validation; the event-driven pub/sub between GlobalChatService and Razor components (with mandatory InvokeAsync wrappers); feature-flag gating so companies can toggle chat on/off; and the BackgroundService that purges messages older than 30 days via CreateScope. It is a full project tutorial, not a theory piece.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: GivingCare's users — caregivers, managers, and administrators scattered across sites and devices — needed an in-app channel that respects the platform's multi-tenancy (no cross-company chatter) and plays nicely with the existing Blazor Server + feature-flag architecture. A third-party integration would have fought the session model; rolling a SignalR-backed module meant the team could reuse ServiceResult, BaseControleContext, and the company-isolation rules already in place. The feature-flag gating also lets companies that don't want chat pay zero runtime cost.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Users see a ChatBadge in the navbar with an unread-count. Clicking opens a ChatDrawer that lists everyone sharing a company with them, with real-time online dots and unread indicators. Picking a user loads a ChatWindow where messages appear live with typing indicators and read receipts (single vs double-check). Messages persist to the ChatMessages table, are purged after 30 days by a BackgroundService, and the entire module can be disabled per company via a Developer-only toggle.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: ChatHub maintains a static ConcurrentDictionary<int, HashSet<string>> of online users and their connection IDs, broadcasting UserOnline only when a user's set transitions from 0 to 1 devices (and UserOffline only on the last disconnect). When a user sends a message, the hub persists via ChatService.SendMessageAsync (which validates shared company membership through UserCompanies), then pushes ReceiveMessage to every recipient connection and MessageSent back to the sender. The client-side GlobalChatService is a scoped singleton-per-circuit that owns the HubConnection, translates hub callbacks into C# events (OnMessageReceived, OnUserTyping, etc.), and exposes them via IGlobalChatService so Razor components can subscribe in OnInitializedAsync and unsubscribe in DisposeAsync. All event handlers must wrap UI updates in InvokeAsync because SignalR callbacks arrive on a thread pool thread, not the Blazor render thread. Typing indicators use a 2-second debounce timer. The ChatCleanupService, a BackgroundService singleton, creates a new scope every 12 hours to resolve the scoped IChatService and delete old rows.

Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.suggested_metaphor: Think of the chat system as a company mailroom: ChatService is the filing cabinet where every letter is kept, ChatHub is the pneumatic tube network that shoots messages across the building in seconds, GlobalChatService is the secretary at each desk who catches the tube and drops letters in the right inbox, and the Razor components are the employees finally reading them. Lose one of the four and the whole building goes silent or floods with paper.
Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.suggested_intro_hook: The trickiest thing about building chat isn't sending messages. It's the user who's logged in on a phone, a laptop, and a tablet at the same time — and still expects exactly one 'online' dot next to their name.
Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.what_it_teaches: How to structure a SignalR-backed feature in Blazor Server across four layers without leaking concerns, how to track multi-device presence correctly, why InvokeAsync is non-negotiable for hub callbacks, and how to wire a BackgroundService that needs scoped dependencies.
key_takeaways: Layer separation is sacred: ChatService holds business logic, ChatHub is a thin relay, Razor is a thin view
ConcurrentDictionary handles key-level concurrency but HashSet values still need their own lock
UserOnline/UserOffline events fire only on first-device connect / last-device disconnect
Every SignalR event handler must wrap UI updates in InvokeAsync() or random render errors appear
BackgroundServices are singletons and must CreateScope() to resolve scoped dependencies
Education/16-SignalR-Chat-System.html.quality_notes: Dense, well-illustrated tutorial. Diagrams for connection lifecycle and message flow are clear. Labelled 'Tutorial #16' of the series. Could use a section on scaling (Redis backplane) but that's beyond its stated scope.

Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.title: Factory Floor Production System: Plain-English Overview
Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.one_line_summary: A non-technical walkthrough of the Factory Floor production tracking system told as a workday narrative, covering the Factory_New page, the Material Consumption modal, and FactoryFloorService.
Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.executive_summary: This infographic-style document explains the Factory Floor system to a non-technical audience using real-world analogies (smart kitchen, video game, restaurant order screen). It introduces the three main components — Factory_New.razor as the worker dashboard, MaterialConsumptionModal.razor as the recipe tracker, and FactoryFloorService.cs as 'the brain' — then walks through a full morning-to-end-of-day scenario with Joao the machine operator showing how start/pause/stop flows, PIN security, material auto-calculation, stock updates, and Primavera accounting integration all chain together.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Paper-based factory tracking loses slips, masks material waste, leaves managers blind until end-of-month reports, and forces double data entry into the accounting system. The Factory Floor module replaces all of that with a tablet-based digital flow that records every start, pause, stop, and material draw the moment it happens, so stock levels, cost accounting, and production KPIs stay in sync with reality instead of trailing it by weeks.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: On a shop-floor tablet, a worker picks their machine, sees Two columns of work orders ('To Start' and 'Started'), and drives each through start -> pause -> material consumption -> stop -> complete, with every action PIN-protected. At pause or stop the Material Consumption modal auto-calculates expected material usage from the quantity produced and historical averages ('last 10 times you made this, you used ~5.2kg'), flags low-stock materials in red, captures waste separately, and posts everything to warehouse stock plus Primavera accounting in one atomic step. Managers watch live stats (units done today, units remaining) on the same dashboard.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Factory_New.razor is the control-center Razor page — it loads open work orders, filters by machine (or GERAL), and shows live status badges. Button clicks (Start/Pause/Stop) call into FactoryFloorService, which validates the PIN, stamps the work order with the operator and timestamp, and moves it between columns. On pause/stop the page opens MaterialConsumptionModal.razor; this modal reads the Bill of Materials for the product, multiplies expected usage by quantity produced, fetches the last N historical runs for comparison, and lets the operator confirm or adjust. On confirm, FactoryFloorService deducts raw materials from stock, credits finished-goods stock, records waste, writes the Primavera accounting entry, and updates the work order's remaining quantity in a single transaction.

Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.suggested_metaphor: The Factory Floor system is the kitchen of a busy restaurant gone digital: Factory_New is the ticket wheel above the pass, the Material Consumption modal is the chef's prep sheet where they tally every gram of flour they actually used, and FactoryFloorService is the sous chef quietly updating inventory, billing, and the reservation screen so nothing gets missed between 'order up!' and 'table paid'.
Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.suggested_intro_hook: Before this system existed, Joao wrote '60 bottles, about 6 kilos of plastic' on a smudged clipboard, someone typed it into accounting three days later, and the warehouse found out it was short on plastic at the worst possible moment. Here's what replaced that.
Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.what_it_teaches: How the factory module fits together from a worker's perspective — which page does what, when the material modal fires, what actions require PIN, and how the three pieces cooperate to keep stock, production, and accounting in lockstep.
key_takeaways: Factory_New is the worker's dashboard; the material modal is the end-of-batch prep sheet; FactoryFloorService is the invisible accountant
Every start, pause, and stop is PIN-logged so nothing is anonymous
Historical averages make material entry one-click for 90% of batches
The system stops an order from starting if stock is insufficient, preventing impossible jobs
One confirm click updates stock, finished goods, and Primavera accounting together
Education/FactoryFloor/ENG/FactoryFloorP.quality_notes: Written as an intentionally non-technical infographic-style overview, so light on code but rich in analogies and user-journey narrative. Ideal as a front-door document for the Factory Floor domain. Not a code tutorial — pair it with the ENG service/modal docs for implementation detail.

CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.title: Cookie Handling in Blazor Server Applications
CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.one_line_summary: A post-mortem on the Blazor Server redirect-loop bug where ASP.NET auto URL-decodes cookies during prerendering while JavaScript does not, breaking the decryption method that assumed encoded input.
CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.executive_summary: This document explains a subtle authentication bug in a Blazor Server app where direct URL access and F5 refresh triggered redirect loops to login, while in-app navigation worked fine. The root cause: ASP.NET's HttpContext.Request.Cookies[] automatically URL-decodes cookies, while JavaScript's document.cookie returns them raw. The team's Decrypt method always called HttpUtility.UrlDecode first, so cookies read via HttpContext during prerendering got double-decoded, corrupted, and failed Base64 validation. The fix registers IHttpContextAccessor, teaches SessionService to detect which source it is reading from, and passes a skipUrlDecode flag into a refactored DecryptData method.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The app had a broken authentication UX: users who typed a URL directly or hit F5 got bounced back to login even though they had a valid session cookie. Clicking a menu link always worked. This inconsistency is a classic Blazor Server prerendering symptom and costs the team constant user complaints, so the team documented the diagnosis and fix as a reference for future bugs in the same neighborhood.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: The fix makes SessionService work correctly regardless of whether it is called during prerendering (no JavaScript yet, must read cookies from HttpContext) or after the circuit is interactive (can call JS getCookie). It does this by injecting IHttpContextAccessor, trying HttpContext first if available, then falling back to JavaScript, and telling the decryption routine which source the ciphertext came from so it knows whether to URL-decode or not.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Step 1: Program.cs calls AddHttpContextAccessor() to make IHttpContextAccessor available in DI. Step 2: SessionService takes IHttpContextAccessor in its constructor. Step 3: DecryptData(string cookieValue, bool skipUrlDecode) branches: if skipUrlDecode is true the raw string is treated as already-decoded base64; otherwise HttpUtility.UrlDecode is applied first, then AES decryption runs. Step 4: GetUserSessionAsync checks an in-memory cache first, then tries _httpContextAccessor.HttpContext?.Request.Cookies['user'] and calls DecryptData with skipUrlDecode:true (because HttpContext already decoded it), and finally falls back to JavaScript interop with skipUrlDecode:false — catching the expected InvalidOperationException thrown when JS isn't yet available during the initial prerender.

CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.suggested_metaphor: It was like receiving a gift-wrapped package at two different doors: the front door (JavaScript) always handed you the box wrapped, and the back door (HttpContext) always unwrapped it for you before handing it over. Your opening routine assumed everything arrived wrapped, so when you tried to 'unwrap' an already-open package you just tore the present to shreds. The fix: ask each delivery door whether it pre-unwrapped it for you.
CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.suggested_intro_hook: The navigation menu worked perfectly. F5 broke everything. That asymmetry is a tell — somewhere in your code, one code path sees the world differently from the other, and in Blazor Server the usual suspect is prerendering.
CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.what_it_teaches: How Blazor Server prerendering changes the rules for anything that touches the browser (cookies, localStorage, window), how to use IHttpContextAccessor to read request state during prerendering, and how to design a dual-source session service that doesn't assume JavaScript is available.
key_takeaways: HttpContext.Request.Cookies auto URL-decodes; document.cookie does not — assume mismatch
During prerendering there is no JavaScript, so any JS interop throws InvalidOperationException
Always test direct URL access, F5 refresh, and in-app navigation separately when debugging auth
Centralise session logic in one service so every page inherits the fix
Detect your cookie source and adapt your decryption — a single rigid path breaks in prerender
CookieHandlingBlazorServerApplications.d.quality_notes: Excellent post-mortem format: problem description, symptom list, root cause table, fix diff, before/after flow, and a troubleshooting cheat sheet at the end. The encoding journey table is particularly clear. Document Version 1.0, dated September 2025.

Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..title: Authorization Architecture
Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..one_line_summary: The GivingCare authorization stack: database-backed UserSystemRole levels, an AuthenticatedComponentBase with cached IsAdminOrAbove-style flags, and a future declarative [RequirePermission] attribute layer.
Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..executive_summary: This document sketches the unified authorization design used in GivingCare across three layers: a database UserSystemRole table with numeric Level values (100 SuperAdmin, 80 Admin, 60 Manager, otherwise Regular), an AuthenticatedComponentBase Blazor base class that resolves the current user's role in OnInitializedAsync and exposes convenience booleans (IsSuperAdmin, IsAdminOrAbove, IsManagerOrAbove), and a planned declarative layer using [RequireSystemRole('ADMIN')] and [RequirePermission('USERS.CREATE')] attributes. It also shows HR-specific config checks (CanClockInOutAsync, CanValidateAttendanceAsync) that read from EmployeeConfiguration rather than the role table.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The codebase needed to centralize authorization checks that were scattered across Razor markup, service methods, and page attributes. Without a unified model, adding a new role meant hunting through dozens of if-user-in-role checks and HR-specific gates (like 'can this person clock in?') were even more ad-hoc. This architecture document lays out the contract that every page and service should follow, plus a migration path toward declarative attributes.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides every authenticated Blazor page with a known set of cached boolean flags (IsSuperAdmin, IsAdminOrAbove, IsManagerOrAbove, RoleLevel) that can gate UI without roundtripping to the database, plus async HR checks (CanClockInOutAsync, CanValidateAttendanceAsync) that read per-employee configuration. Services use AuthorizationService.CanUserPerformAction as the final gate before mutating state, and pages will soon use [RequireSystemRole('ADMIN')] as a route-level filter.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Page level: @attribute [RequireSystemRole('ADMIN')] (future) uses a policy-based AuthorizeAttribute mapped to 'SystemRole:ADMIN'. Component level: @if (IsAdminOrAbove) wraps optional UI — the booleans come from AuthenticatedComponentBase which calls AuthorizationService.GetUserRoleAsync(UserId) once in OnInitializedAsync. That service queries UserSystemRoles joined to Role, filters to IsActive, orders by Level desc, and bucketises into the UserRole enum via a switch expression on Role.Level. Service layer: each mutation calls _auth.CanUserPerformAction(userId) and returns ServiceResult.Failure('Unauthorized') if it returns false. HR checks take a different route: they look up EmployeeConfiguration by LinkedEmployeeId and read the FazPicagens / ValidaPicagens flags instead of using the role table.

Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..suggested_metaphor: The authorization stack is like airport security in three tiers: the page-level [RequireSystemRole] is the TSA pre-check at the entrance (if you fail here you never even see the gate), the component-level IsAdminOrAbove is the gate agent hiding first-class lounge access behind a velvet rope, and the service-level CanUserPerformAction is the flight attendant who checks your ticket one last time before letting you into the cockpit. You want all three — any single one alone leaves a door open.
Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..suggested_intro_hook: A junior dev once shipped an 'Admin Only' button hidden with CSS. The button was still in the DOM, and a motivated user deleted the entire customer database with one click. That is why authorization never ends at the UI layer.
Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..what_it_teaches: How to structure authorization across Blazor pages, components, and services so that role checks are consistent, cached, and impossible to bypass — plus how to handle feature-specific permissions (HR clock-in, attendance validation) that don't fit neatly into a role level.
key_takeaways: Never rely on a single layer — UI-level hiding, component-level flags, and service-level checks are defense in depth
Cache role lookups in a base class (OnInitializedAsync) so every @if check is local
Numeric role levels (100/80/60) make >= comparisons readable and easy to extend with intermediate tiers
HR-style capability checks belong in EmployeeConfiguration, not the role table
Declarative [RequireSystemRole] attributes give you route-level enforcement with no code duplication
Education/04-Authorization-Architecture..quality_notes: Concise architecture note (~540 words) — more of an overview than a deep dive. The 'Future' section on declarative attributes is clearly forward-looking. Would benefit from concrete examples of the AuthorizationService.CanUserPerformAction signature, and a note on how assigner-role validation actually works in AssignRoleToUserAsync.

Education/login.html.title: Animated Character Login Page (Interactive Demo)
Education/login.html.one_line_summary: A self-contained HTML demo of a login form where three SVG bird/duck characters track the cursor, cover their eyes when the password field focuses, and celebrate or frown based on authentication outcome — driven entirely by a CSS state-machine class on the root element.
Education/login.html.executive_summary: This is an interactive design prototype, not a written tutorial. A purple bird, a black bird, and a yellow duck sit beside a login form and react to user input via a state machine: their pupils track the mouse in s-idle/s-email states, they smile when the email validates, frown when it doesn't, raise both arms to cover their eyes in the s-password state, drop one arm for the s-peek state (show-password toggle), bounce in s-success, and shake in s-error. The entire state machine is implemented by toggling a single class (s-idle, s-email, s-password, s-peek, s-success, s-error) on #app and letting targeted CSS rules do the animation via display toggles and cubic-bezier transforms.
key_concepts: pupil cursor tracking with viewBox math

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: A UX inspiration piece — the developer wanted to explore how much personality a login page could have without using a heavy framework. The characters make a dry authentication screen feel alive and give the user immediate, pre-submit feedback about email validity and password visibility state, which is both delightful and a subtle trust signal.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Renders a two-panel card: a beige character panel on the left with three SVG characters, and a form panel on the right with email, password, remember-me, login button, and Google SSO button. As the user types and focuses fields, the characters animate: they watch the cursor, smile at valid emails, frown at invalid ones, cover their eyes while you type your password (except for a peeking character when show-password is on), bounce for successful login, and shake on errors. The submit is simulated client-side (success if password length >= 6).
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The root div has id='app' and a class like 's-idle' that acts as the state label. JavaScript listens to focus/input/blur events on the email and password inputs and on the login button, calling setState(name) which just rewrites app.className = 's-' + name. From there, everything is CSS: selectors like '#app.s-password .arm-left { transform: translateY(-190px); }' translate arms up, '#app.s-email-ok .e-smile { display: block; }' swap expression groups, and '#app.s-success .c-purple { animation: bounce 0.8s ease both; }' runs keyframes. Pupil tracking is a single mousemove listener that, if the current state is in the TRACKING_STATES set, converts clientX/clientY into the SVG's viewBox coordinates using getBoundingClientRect and vb.width/vb.height, then clamps each pupil's offset to its max range. A small helper toggleShowPw swaps input.type and the eye icon SVG path data.

Education/login.html.suggested_metaphor: The state machine here is like a mood ring for the whole page: change one class on the root element and the entire visual tone shifts — expressions appear, arms jump, pupils dilate — all because the CSS file is a giant 'if the ring is red, be angry; if it is blue, be calm' rulebook. You never have to touch the SVG from JavaScript at all.
Education/login.html.suggested_intro_hook: Every login form has the same three fields and the same two buttons. What if the form watched you type and reacted like a nervous pet? This demo is 600 lines of HTML that makes a dead-serious auth screen actually fun to look at.
Education/login.html.what_it_teaches: How to build a CSS-driven state machine by toggling a class on the root element, how to make SVG pupils track the cursor with proper viewBox math, and how to swap character expressions using display-block/none on nested SVG groups rather than rewriting paths from JavaScript.
key_takeaways: One class on the root + targeted selectors = a full state machine with zero per-element JS toggling
SVG cursor tracking needs viewBox-to-pixel scaling via getBoundingClientRect, not raw clientX/Y
Expression swapping via display:none on pre-drawn <g> groups is cleaner than animating paths
cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) gives arm movement a springy 'overshoot' that feels alive
Show-password state should be its own state (s-peek) so the character's reaction mirrors the user's action
Education/login.html.quality_notes: The text extraction is nearly empty (27 words) because this is an interactive HTML demo with no narrative copy, only inline CSS, SVG, and a script tag. Analysis here is based on reading the actual source rather than the extracted text. It is a valuable 'design reference' artefact rather than an educational doc per se — treat it as a demo/example rather than a tutorial and link it from a UI-patterns or login-page topic page.

Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.title: C# Deep Dive: Generics, Builders & Everything In Between
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.one_line_summary: A nine-part walkthrough that builds up from generic type parameters to a full functional builder pattern, weaving together constraints, recursive generics, interface masking, extension methods, delegates as data, and Aggregate.
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.executive_summary: This deep dive teaches the C# generics machinery by progressively assembling a Functional Builder pattern. It starts from the simplest Box<T> idea, then layers on constraints (where T : new()), recursive generics for fluent chaining (class Child : Parent<Child>), interface return types as 'masks' that enforce method ordering, extension methods, delegates stored in lists, and finally LINQ's Aggregate as the assembly line that runs every stored action against a fresh instance. The payoff is understanding why FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf> is the way it is, and being able to read every line of it.
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.suggested_metaphor: Generics are a shipping label with a blank field, constraints are the fine print under the blank, recursive generics are a relay race where the parent always hands the baton back to the right team, interfaces are masks that hide every face except the one you want the caller to see, and Aggregate is the factory assembly line that walks a blank chassis past every station until a finished car rolls out the other end.
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.suggested_intro_hook: If you have ever stared at where TSelf : FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf> and felt like you were reading a C# tongue-twister, this is the doc that finally makes you hear the music in it. Every weird angle bracket is doing a job, and once you see the jobs, the whole thing reads like prose.
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.what_it_teaches: How to read and write advanced generic signatures in C#, when each constraint earns its keep, how to keep fluent builder chains type-safe across inheritance, how interfaces can be used as 'view restrictions' to enforce a call order, how extension methods let you grow a sealed class from outside, how to store behavior in lists for later replay, and how Aggregate compresses a foreach loop with an accumulator into a single line.
key_takeaways: T is a placeholder filled in at use-site, and constraints are the contract that lets the compiler trust you
Recursive generics exist purely so a parent class can return the child's type for fluent chaining
Returning an interface lets you hide methods and force a step order on the caller
Builders that store Func<T,T> in a list are just recipe books; nothing runs until Build() reads the book
Aggregate is a one-line foreach that walks a list and carries an accumulator
Education/generics-builders-deep-dive.ht.quality_notes: Excellent pedagogical structure: each part introduces one concept with a metaphor, then connects it to the running FunctionalBuilder example. Includes a practice exercise section with answers and a quick reference card at the end. One of the best teaching docs in the library.

JScript/Document 1.docx.title: jQuery, Select2 and AG Grid Custom Editors/Filters - Method Breakdown
JScript/Document 1.docx.one_line_summary: A line-by-line breakdown of a jQuery + Select2 initialization function, an AG Grid CustomSelectEditor and a CustomTextFilter, explaining what each piece does and flagging the focus/event-handling pitfalls.
JScript/Document 1.docx.executive_summary: This document walks through three pieces of legacy frontend code in painful detail: an initializeSelect2() helper that defensively sets up Select2 dropdowns with Portuguese localization, an AG Grid CustomSelectEditor that wires Select2 into editable grid cells, and a CustomTextFilter that recreates AG Grid's text filter with Portuguese labels and an enhanced array-column filter. Beyond the explanations, the doc calls out four bugs in the editor (global selectors causing focus to jump between Select2 instances, overly broad event.stopPropagation, dropdownParent: document.body issues, opening Select2 before init), making it half tutorial and half code review.
builds_toward: migrating jQuery widgets to vanilla JS
JScript/Document 1.docx.suggested_metaphor: Reading this doc is like watching a mechanic with a paint marker circle every loose bolt on a working car. The car drives, but you would not want to take it onto the highway: a global $('.select2-search__field').focus() is the one bolt that will fly off and hit somebody.
JScript/Document 1.docx.suggested_intro_hook: Ever wonder why your fancy AG Grid Select2 editor steals focus from a totally different cell halfway across the screen? It is almost always the same one-line bug, and this doc shows you the exact line.
JScript/Document 1.docx.what_it_teaches: How a real Select2 + AG Grid integration is wired up method-by-method, why each AG Grid lifecycle hook (init, getGui, afterGuiAttached, getValue, destroy, isPopup) exists, and how to build a custom filter with state restoration. Equally importantly, it teaches what NOT to do: global jQuery selectors inside per-instance code, blanket stopPropagation, and racing the Select2 init.
key_takeaways: Always namespace your jQuery selectors to the current instance, never use document-wide selectors inside per-cell editors
AG Grid custom editors must implement init/getGui/getValue/destroy and return true from isPopup() for popup-style editors
Custom filters need getModel/setModel so AG Grid can save and restore filter state
Defensive checks like if ($.fn.select2 === undefined) keep pages from crashing when a CDN dependency fails to load
JScript/Document 1.docx.quality_notes: Surprisingly thorough. Reads like a code review notebook with both the 'what does this do' and 'this is broken because' commentary inline. The Portuguese localization context makes it clearly tied to a real legacy project. No diagrams, just pasted snippets.

Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.title: SignalR Real-Time Communication in Blazor Server
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.one_line_summary: End-to-end SignalR walkthrough for Blazor Server: build the Hub, build the IHubContext-based service, register everything in Program.cs, connect from a Razor component, and use Groups to scope notifications to companies and teams.
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.executive_summary: This doc is a complete recipe for adding SignalR real-time updates to a Blazor Server app. It covers the full loop: Hub class with OnConnectedAsync/OnDisconnectedAsync and JoinGroup/LeaveGroup methods, a HubService that uses IHubContext to push messages without holding a connection, Program.cs registration, and a fully wired Blazor component with HubConnectionBuilder, automatic reconnect, group rejoin on Reconnected, message handlers registered before StartAsync, and IAsyncDisposable cleanup. The most valuable part is the bug-hunting section: 'wrong event name' is named the #1 cause of 'SignalR not working,' along with the group-name mismatch trap (Team_null_1) and the rule that StateHasChanged on a parent does NOT re-init child components.
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.suggested_metaphor: A SignalR Hub is a CB radio in the middle of the warehouse. Groups are channels: every connection that joins 'Company_1' hears the foreman's announcements, while only people who joined 'Team_5_1' hear the shift leader. The Hub does not remember which channels you were on after a reconnect, so the very first thing your component must do when the radio crackles back to life is shout out 'Joining Channel 1 again!' or your dashboard will silently go deaf.
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.suggested_intro_hook: You add SignalR, you push the message, and... nothing happens on the dashboard. You stare at the code, you stare at the network tab, you stare at the dog. Nine times out of ten, the bug is one of three things, and this doc names all three.
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.what_it_teaches: How to wire SignalR end-to-end in Blazor Server, how to use Groups to target broadcasts at exactly the right audience (company vs team vs single user), and how to avoid the five classic SignalR bugs: wrong event name on the .On() handler, missing rejoin after reconnect, missing InvokeAsync wrap on StateHasChanged, registering handlers after StartAsync, and not telling child components to refresh.
key_takeaways: Hubs receive client calls, HubServices push messages from server-side code via IHubContext<T>
Group names are strings - any mismatch (e.g. Team_null_1) silently routes messages into the void
SignalR forgets your group memberships on disconnect; rejoin them in the Reconnected handler
Always wrap StateHasChanged in InvokeAsync inside SignalR callbacks to marshal back to the UI thread
Initialize SignalR in OnAfterRenderAsync, not OnInitializedAsync, so NavigationManager is ready
Education/11-SignalR-Real-Time-Communica.quality_notes: Production-grade reference doc. Includes ASCII diagrams of the message flow, a 'common issues' table that maps symptoms to fixes, and explicit WRONG vs CORRECT code blocks. Ties to real implementation files (AttendanceHub) at the end. Numbered prefix '11-' suggests it is part of a larger Education series.

Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.title: Sistema de Produção de Chão de Fábrica - Documentação Técnica (PT)
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.one_line_summary: Portuguese-language formal technical documentation for the Factory Floor MES system, covering its layered architecture, Factory_New.razor and MaterialConsumptionModal components, the FactoryFloorService and its Primavera ERP integration.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.executive_summary: This is the formal Portuguese-language technical doc for the BioBraga Factory Floor system - a real-time MES (Manufacturing Execution System) built on Blazor Server, MudBlazor, EF Core, and integrated with the Primavera ERP. It documents the layered architecture (Presentation -> Service -> Data Access), the Factory_New.razor and MaterialConsumptionModal.razor components with their lifecycle methods, the IFactoryFloorService interface and its key operations (StartProductionAsync, PauseProductionAsync, EndProductionAsync, RegisterProductionAsync), the proportional material consumption algorithm with historical average suggestion, the multi-step transactional flow that updates order quantities, registers material consumption, and generates ENTSTOCK/SAIDASTOCK/DESP stock movement documents, plus PIN-based worker authentication and the 1.5s debounce on quantity-change material loading.
key_concepts: proportional material consumption with historical average
builds_toward: extending the system with new machine types

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: A real factory needs to know in real time which production orders are running on which machines, how much material was actually consumed (versus planned), and how much waste was generated - and every one of those facts has to flow back into the Primavera ERP so inventory and accounting stay consistent. Without this system, the floor relied on paper logs and the ERP saw stale data; with it, the worker scans a PIN, reports actual quantities, and the system writes the order update, the material consumption, the stock movements, and the ERP push in a single transaction.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides a touch-friendly Blazor UI (Factory_New.razor) where workers see all active production orders filtered by their machine, then via PIN authentication can Start, Pause or End an order. Pause/End opens the MaterialConsumptionModal which loads materials proportionally to the reported quantity, shows historical-average suggestions and live variance, validates stock availability, and on submit walks a multi-step progress UI (update order, register consumption, generate stock entry, generate stock exit, push to Primavera, finalize). Includes today's production stats and machine filtering via URL parameters for bookmarkability.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Layered: Razor components inject IFactoryFloorService, which uses IDbContextFactory<BioBragaContext> to open scoped DB contexts and IPrimaveraRepository for ERP calls. The material algorithm is perUnit = totalPlanned / orderQuantity, then proportionalQty = perUnit * quantityProduced rounded to 6 decimals, with an optional historical-average suggestion when QuantidadeMedia is non-zero. RegisterProductionAsync wraps everything in BeginTransactionAsync: it bumps QuantidadeFeita/QuantidadeFalta on the order, increments QuantidadeConsumida and NumeroProducoes on each gastoFase, generates CrmDocumento headers and lines for ENTSTOCK/SAIDASTOCK/DESP, then commits or rolls back. Material loading uses CancellationTokenSource debouncing (1.5s) so users can retype the produced quantity without hammering the DB. PIN auth hashes via Utils.Hash and rejects inactive workers.

Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.suggested_metaphor: The Factory Floor system is the invisible accountant standing next to every machine on the shop floor. The worker says 'I made 47 units and used this much glue,' the accountant whispers 'that is 8% over the plan, here is what your last 12 batches averaged,' then quietly walks the paperwork over to the ERP filing cabinet so nobody has to retype anything later.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.suggested_intro_hook: What does it actually take to turn 'the worker pressed the green button' into a row in the ERP that finance trusts? It takes a PIN screen, a debounced material loader, a five-step transaction, and the patience to roll all of it back if Primavera coughs.
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.what_it_teaches: How a real MES module is layered in Blazor Server, how to compose a transactional service that touches local DB and an external ERP without leaving inconsistent state, and how to design a UX that surfaces variance against historical averages so the worker (not just the manager) becomes a quality sensor.
key_takeaways: IDbContextFactory plus an existingContext parameter lets the same service method participate in a caller-owned transaction or open its own
Debouncing material loads via CancellationTokenSource is what keeps the UI usable when the user is still typing the quantity
Proportional + historical-average suggestion gives workers a sanity-check before they confirm consumption
Stock movement creation must be inside the same transaction as the order update or the ERP and DB will drift
URL-parameter machine selection makes the floor view bookmarkable without server roundtrips for filtering
Education/FactoryFloor/PT/SistemaProduçã.quality_notes: Formal documentation style in Portuguese (PT-PT). Well structured with sections for architecture, components, services, data models, integration, security, performance, deployment. Code snippets are realistic and the transaction flow is described concretely. This is the PT counterpart to the FactoryFloor English docs - same domain, separate page so the Portuguese version is also browsable.

Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.title: Design Patterns & SOLID Principles - For Dummies (Schedule Conflict Detector)
Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.one_line_summary: Walks through how the schedule conflict detector was refactored using Interface, Strategy, DI with IEnumerable<T>, and Facade patterns, mapping each step to its SOLID principle - starting from the real problem of needing the same conflict logic for Employees, Equipment and (later) Vehicles.
Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.executive_summary: This doc tells the story of a real refactor: the team had a scheduling conflict detector that only handled Employees, then Equipment was added, and Vehicles were on the horizon. Instead of copy-pasting, they built an IScheduleEntry interface for the row shape, an IScheduleConflictStrategy interface for the per-entity-type query, registered both Employee and Equipment strategies in DI as IEnumerable<T>, and put a ScheduleConflictDetector facade in front so callers just say HasTimeOverlapAsync('Employee', 123, ...). Each step is tied to a SOLID letter (ISP, OCP, DIP, SRP), and the payoff section shows that adding Vehicles is now 'create class, register, done, no existing code changes.'
key_concepts: IEnumerable<T> DI to collect all implementations
prerequisites: the basic problem of code duplication

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The scheduling system originally only handled Employees, but the same 'does this overlap with anything I am already booked for' logic was needed for Equipment, and Vehicles were coming next. Without a refactor, every entity type meant another full copy of EmployeeConflictService, with bugs to fix in N places and features to add in N places. The doc is the team's record of how they made the third entity type cheap.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Lets any caller ask 'does Entity X with id Y have a scheduling conflict in this time window?' without knowing or caring what type X is. Internally it routes the question to the right per-type query strategy and uses a shared row interface so the overlap math works against either JobSchedules or JobEquipmentSchedules with the same code path.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: Both JobSchedule and JobEquipmentSchedule implement IScheduleEntry (ActualStartDateTime, ActualEndDateTime, OverlapsWith). For each entity type there is a class that implements IScheduleConflictStrategy with EntityType property and HasConflictAsync method that queries the right table. All strategies are registered in DI as IScheduleConflictStrategy, so injecting IEnumerable<IScheduleConflictStrategy> gives you the full collection. The ScheduleConflictDetector facade does .First(s => s.EntityType == requestedType) and delegates. Adding Vehicle means: implement IScheduleEntry on JobVehicleSchedule, write VehicleScheduleConflictStrategy, register it - existing files untouched.

Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.suggested_metaphor: Picture a customs office at an airport with one window for citizens, one for residents, and one for tourists. Each clerk (strategy) only knows how to look up their own kind of traveler in their own database. The information desk (facade) just asks 'what kind are you?' and points you at the right window. Adding a new visa class means hiring one new clerk - the desk and the other windows do not need to change at all.
Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.suggested_intro_hook: If your first instinct when adding Equipment scheduling was 'I will just copy EmployeeConflictService and rename it,' read this. There is a version of you six months from now whose job is much easier if you spend forty minutes on patterns today.
Education/ForDummies/08-Design-Patterns-.what_it_teaches: How to recognize when to introduce Strategy + Facade + DI collection, how the SOLID letters map onto each step of the refactor (not as theory, but as the named justification for each decision), and what the actual payoff looks like when you add the third entity type.
key_takeaways: If you find yourself about to copy-paste a service to support a new entity type, that is the moment Strategy pays off
Injecting IEnumerable<IInterface> in .NET DI gives you every registered implementation as a collection - no service locator needed
A Facade keeps callers ignorant of the strategy lookup, which is itself the SRP win
OCP is real: 'open for extension, closed for modification' is exactly what 'no existing files change' looks like in practice
ISP means the shared interface should only carry what the cross-cutting code actually needs - not the full entity

Education/ForDummies/14-SignalR-Notifica.one_line_summary: Beginner walkthrough of the multi-target notification system: how to address messages by Group, Department, Job/Project or Role, how SignalR groups auto-join on connect, why offline users still get the message, and what the EnvioGlobal sender UI looks like.
Education/ForDummies/14-SignalR-Notifica.executive_summary: Part 2 of the SignalR ForDummies pair. Introduces the notification system as a 'shopping mall PA system' with multiple targeting tabs (Grupos, Departamentos, Obras, Funcoes), explains the address-resolution chain (target -> employees -> users), walks through how every connected user is auto-joined to several SignalR groups (User_*, All, Company_*, Dept_*, Job_*, Role_*), explains the offline 'voicemail' fallback where notifications are persisted in the database for later, and walks through the four-step EnvioGlobal sender UI. Designed for someone who has never used SignalR before.
key_concepts: Blazor UI vs REST controller dual-entry

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The team needed to push notifications to many different audiences - not just user groups, but everyone in a department, everyone working on a project, everyone with a particular job title - and they needed both Blazor pages and external systems (mobile, integrations, background jobs) to be able to fire those notifications. They also could not afford to lose messages just because the recipient was offline at the moment of sending.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Lets a sender pick a target type (Grupo, Departamento, Obra, Funcao), pick the specific targets, type a title and message, and send. The system resolves each target to a deduplicated list of users, delivers via SignalR to whoever is online right now, and persists the rest so offline users see them on next login. Both Blazor (INotificationService) and REST (POST /api/notification/send-to-department) entry points exist.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: When a user connects, the system auto-joins their connection to several SignalR groups: their personal User_* group, the global All group, their Company_* group, their Dept_*_* group, every Job_*_* group they belong to, and their Role_*_* group. To deliver a message, the sender names a target type and ID; the system queries the company DB for the matching employees, then queries the central DB to find which users those employees correspond to, dedupes, and pushes via the relevant group. Online users receive instantly via the existing connection; offline users get a database row that surfaces on next login - the 'voicemail' fallback.

When the manager wants to call the IT department to a meeting, she does not need every shopper's name - she just keys the IT channel and only the IT walkie-talkies crackle. key_takeaways: SignalR groups are addressable channels - join one and you hear everything broadcast on it
Multi-target notification works by resolving each target tab into a deduplicated user list before broadcasting
Offline does not mean lost: notifications persist to the DB and surface on next login
The same notification engine should expose both an in-process service (for Blazor) and a REST controller (for mobile/integrations)
Auto-joining a user to multiple groups on connect is what makes targeting cheap at send time

Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.title: Generics in C#: A Comprehensive Guide
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.one_line_summary: A full tour of C# generics from the pre-generics pain of ArrayList boxing to advanced topics like reification, variance, constraints, and reflection over open generic types.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.executive_summary: This is an end-to-end reference on C# generics that starts with the historical motivation (boxing penalties and lost type safety in object-based collections) and walks through generic classes, methods, interfaces, constraints, variance, static members per constructed type, reflection, and idiomatic patterns like Repository, Factory, Specification, and Result. Its standout insight is the contrast between Java's type erasure and C#'s reification — the CLR preserves generic type information at runtime, which is why frameworks like EF Core, DI containers, and serializers can do the things they do. The guide closes with practical usage in EF Core, open-generic DI registration, and Blazor @typeparam components.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.suggested_metaphor: Generics are like a pasta machine with swappable dies. The machine itself is one design — feed dough in and turn the crank — but you snap a different die on top and out comes spaghetti, rigatoni, or fettuccine. The List<T> class is that one machine; List<int> and List<Employee> are the pasta shapes you get when you choose the die. Boxing in the old ArrayList world was like shoving every noodle into an unlabelled tupperware and then guessing what shape it was when you opened it later.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.suggested_intro_hook: In 2004, you couldn't put an integer in a .NET collection without boxing it onto the heap and unboxing it on the way out — a tax you paid in every tight loop. Then C# 2.0 shipped, and suddenly the List<int> you wrote was literally a different type in memory than List<string>. This guide explains what that actually means and why it's still the most impactful feature to understand in modern .NET.
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.what_it_teaches: How generics work at the language level, runtime level (reification), and idiomatic level (patterns). It covers every constraint flavour, the variance rules, how static state is per-constructed-type, and how to use reflection to build generic types dynamically.
key_takeaways: C# generics are reified at runtime, not erased — the CLR knows the exact type arguments and can generate specialised value-type code without boxing
Constraints are promises to the compiler about what T can do, which unlocks operations like CompareTo, new T(), or casting to null
Covariance (out) is safe when T only leaves the type; contravariance (in) is safe when T only enters the type; anything else must be invariant
Static fields in a generic class are per constructed type — Counter<int>.Count and Counter<string>.Count are independent slots
Open generic registrations let DI containers resolve IRepository<T> for any T with a single line of configuration
Education/Basics/CSharp_Generics_Guide.p.quality_notes: Dense, well-structured, and genuinely comprehensive. Covers historical context, syntax, constraints, variance, reflection, and ecosystem usage — unusual for a single document to hit all of those without becoming shallow. Code samples are realistic and include the patterns a .NET developer will actually encounter. Minor formatting artifacts from PDF extraction (line breaks inside code blocks) but readable.

JScript/JS_Select2&CustomMethods.pdf.one_line_summary: A line-by-line tour of three JavaScript building blocks — initializing Select2 with jQuery, a custom AG Grid cell editor, and a custom AG Grid text filter — with Portuguese localisation and a running critique of the editor's focus bugs.
JScript/JS_Select2&CustomMethods.pdf.executive_summary: The document decomposes three JavaScript routines used in a legacy Blazor/jQuery hybrid app. The first explains initializeSelect2 and the jQuery document-ready pattern — why $.fn.select2 is guarded before use, why jQuery(document).ready wraps initialisation, and the modern ES6 alternatives. The second is a full dissection of a CustomSelectEditor class for AG Grid (prototype methods: init, getGui, afterGuiAttached, getValue, destroy, isPopup, onKeyDown) including four annotated bugs around dropdownParent, event propagation, and the global $('.select2-search__field') selector that steals focus across instances. The third walks through a CustomTextFilter with AG Grid styling, Portuguese labels, and a full filter-state lifecycle (init, doesFilterPass, getModel, setModel, event handlers).
JScript/JS_Select2&CustomMethods.pdf.suggested_metaphor: AG Grid's cell editor contract is like a relay race. AG Grid hands you the baton at init, watches you run the lap inside the cell with afterGuiAttached, takes the baton back with getValue, and finally retires you at destroy. If you don't return the baton cleanly — because you stopPropagation on every click or grab focus with a global selector — the next runner trips and the whole race looks glitchy.
JScript/JS_Select2&CustomMethods.pdf.suggested_intro_hook: Why does clicking a dropdown in one row sometimes steal the keyboard focus from a dropdown in another row? JScript/JS_Select2&CustomMethods.pdf.what_it_teaches: How to read and write Select2 initialization safely, how AG Grid's cell-editor lifecycle fits together, how to build a custom AG Grid text filter that follows the expected contract (getModel/setModel/doesFilterPass), and what pitfalls make custom editors feel buggy (over-broad event stopping, global selectors, focus races).
key_takeaways: Always guard optional libraries ($.fn.select2 === undefined) before calling into them — fail fast with a clear error instead of a mysterious crash
jQuery(document).ready(function($) {...}) gives you an explicit, conflict-proof $ scoped to your block, even if another library has stolen the global $
AG Grid cell editors follow a strict lifecycle: init -> getGui -> afterGuiAttached -> getValue -> destroy; each method has a specific job and skipping one creates weird bugs
Global jQuery selectors like $('.select2-search__field') inside a per-row component are a focus-stealing footgun — always scope to the instance
Custom AG Grid filters must implement isFilterActive, doesFilterPass, getModel, setModel as a matched set; missing one breaks state persistence

Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.title: Base Entity Abstractions & Soft Delete
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.one_line_summary: A layered inheritance tree (BaseEntity -> BaseAuditableEntity -> BaseSoftDeletableEntity) combined with IAuditable/ISoftDeletable interfaces and EF Core HasQueryFilter to give 45+ domain models audit tracking and soft delete with zero per-entity boilerplate.
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.executive_summary: This tutorial shows how to use abstract base classes as nesting dolls — each level adds fields without re-declaring what came before — so every entity in a large codebase inherits an Id, four audit fields, and three soft-delete fields without copy-paste. The twist is pairing the base classes with IAuditable and ISoftDeletable interfaces so EF Core interceptors can pattern-match against any entity type and stamp audit data automatically. The second half walks through HasQueryFilter (global soft-delete filter), the HashSet<Type> blocklist pattern for preventing central-only configs from leaking into tenant contexts in a multi-context setup, modelBuilder.Ignore<T>() for orphan navigation types, and a global cascade-delete disable that forces services to handle deletion order explicitly.
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.suggested_metaphor: The base class hierarchy is a set of Russian nesting dolls. The smallest doll is BaseEntity — it just has an ID, nothing else. Open it and inside sits BaseAuditableEntity, which adds 'who created/modified me' fields. Open that and you find BaseSoftDeletableEntity with 'am I pretending to be deleted?' on top. The biggest doll contains all the others — its 8 properties come from 3 levels of inheritance — but the class file only declares the 3 new ones. Change the innermost doll, every outer one updates automatically.
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.suggested_intro_hook: Forty-five entity classes, each needing the same eight properties. You could paste them in 45 times and pray nobody mistypes 'CreatedAt'. Or you could build a three-level inheritance chain that gives every domain model audit tracking and soft delete for free — with one interceptor that doesn't know any of them by name. This is how.
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.what_it_teaches: How to structure a .NET domain model so that common concerns (ID, audit, soft delete) live in base classes and interfaces, how EF Core's HasQueryFilter makes soft delete invisible to business code, how ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly auto-discovers IEntityTypeConfiguration classes, and how a blocklist pattern keeps multi-database configurations from crossing contexts.
key_takeaways: Inherit from the most specific base you actually need — BaseEntity for lookup tables, BaseAuditableEntity for append-only, BaseSoftDeletableEntity for business records
Interfaces (IAuditable, ISoftDeletable) are what interceptors pattern-match against — the base classes provide reuse, the interfaces provide polymorphism
HasQueryFilter(e => !e.IsDeleted) applies globally to every query including .Include() chains; use .IgnoreQueryFilters() only in admin/recovery code
Disable cascade delete globally (DeleteBehavior.NoAction) to prevent mass-deletion accidents — services should handle deletion order explicitly
In multi-context setups, a HashSet<Type> blocklist fed to ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly's predicate cleanly prevents central-only configurations from being applied to tenant contexts
Education/27-Base-Entity-Abstractions-So.quality_notes: Excellent. Clear progression from why to how, covers the full ecosystem (base classes, interfaces, configurations, interceptors, cascade prevention), and the step-by-step 'Creating a New Entity' section ties the whole thing to a concrete workflow.
